Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:38:39.543+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Courtier, Grand Master for Court Discussion, Right Remonstrance Grand Master, Acting Palace Censor, concurrently Commissioner for Judicial Review, Superior Protector of the Army, bestowed with the purple robe and golden fish pouch,
by imperial decree compiled
Later Student Tiāntāi
The Erya states: When the Great Year is in Jiǎ, it is called Yānpéng;
in Yǐ, Zhānméng;
in Bǐng, Róuzhào;
in Dīng, Qiángyǔ;
in Wù, Zhùyōng;
in Jǐ, Túwéi;
in Gēng, Shàngzhāng;
in Xīn, Chóngguāng;
in Rén, Xuányì;
in Guǐ, Zhāoyáng;
these are the Year Yang.
In Yín, it is called Shètítígé;
in Mǎo, Chányān;
in Chén, Zhíxú;
in Sì, Dàhuāngluò;
in Wǔ, Dūnzāng;
in Wèi, Xiéqià;
in Shēn, Tūntān;
in Yǒu, Zuò'è;
in Xū, Yǎnmào;
in Hài, Dàyuānxiàn;
in Zǐ, Kùndūn;
in Chǒu, Chìfènruò;
these are the Year Names.
The Zhou Annals with separate annotations
"beginning from Zhùyōng Shètítígé"
means beginning from Wùyín.
"ending at Xuányì Kùndūn"
means ending at Rénzǐ.
Yān,
read as the character;
the Records of the Grand Historian writes
"Yān",
pronounced Yúqián fān.
Zhù,
Chénrú fān.
Yōng,
Yúróng fān.
Yì,
Yìzhí fān.
Chányān,
the first character pronounced Dān,
also Tèlián fān;
the second character Wūgě fān,
also Yúlián fān.
Zāng,
Zuòláng fān.
Tūn,
Tǔhún fān.
Tān,
Tǔdān fān.
Kùndūn,
pronounced Dùn.
Dù Yù's Genealogical Records of Clans states: The Zhōu,
descendants of the Yellow Emperor,
surname Jī.
Descendants of Hòujì,
enfeoffed at Tái;
when the Xià declined,
Hòujì's son Bùzhú fled to the Western Róng.
By the twelfth generation descendant, Tàiwáng,
avoiding the Dí, moved to Qí;
by his grandson King Wén received the Mandate,
King Wǔ defeated Shāng and possessed the realm.
From King Wǔ to King Píng were thirteen generations in total,
from King Píng to King Wèiliè were another eighteen generations,
from King Wèiliè to King Nǎn were another five generations.
Zhāng Shǒujié states: Because Tàiwáng resided in Zhōuyuán,
the state was named Zhōu.
The Treatise on Geography states: In the Zhōngshuǐ township northwest of Qí Mountain in Měiyáng county, Right Fǔfēng commandery,
was the city of Zhōu Tàiwáng.
The Expanded Records of Geography states: The old Zhōu city, also named Měiyáng city,
is located twenty-five lǐ northwest of Wǔgōng county in Yōngzhōu.
Annals,
means to order,
to systematically order all affairs and connect them to years and months.
Master Wēn's chronological compilation uses the method of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
following the basic annals of the Historian and the Han and calling them Annals.
Tái,
Tānglái fān.
Xià,
Hùyǎ fān.
Zhú,
Zhúzhú fān.
In Yōng,
Yúyòng fān.
King Wèiliè
personal name Wǔ,
son of King Kǎo.
The Canon of Posthumous Titles states: Fierce and resolute is called Wèi;
having merit and pacifying the people is called Liè.
Shěn Yuē states: For all compound posthumous titles,
there are people who received them,
but no codified rules for them.
1 First, he appointed the Jìn grand masters Wèi Sī, Zhào Jí, and Hán Qián as feudal lords.
This is the origin of Master Wēn's historical method.
The ancestors of Wèi,
descendants of Duke Bì Gāo,
were of the same surname as Zhōu;
their descendant was called Bì Wàn,
first enfeoffed at Wèi.
Down to Wèi Shū,
he first became the chief minister of Jìn;
three generations later to Sī.
The ancestors of Zhào,
descendants of Zàofù;
down to Shūdài,
he first moved from Zhōu to Jìn;
down to Zhào Sù,
he was first enfeoffed at Gěng.
Down to Zhào Dùn,
he first became the chief minister of Jìn;
six generations later to Jí.
The ancestors of Hán,
descended from King Wǔ of Zhōu;
down to Hán Wǔzǐ, he served Jìn,
and was enfeoffed at Hányuán.
Down to Hán Jué,
he became the chief minister of Jìn;
six generations later to Qián.
These three families,
for generations were grand masters of Jìn,
in relation to Zhōu, they were subsidiary ministers.
The Zhōu house having already declined,
Jìn presided over the alliances of the Xià region,
in order to honor the royal house,
therefore they were appointed as Hegemons.
The three ministers usurped the authority of Jìn,
outrageously scorned their lord,
and carved up his state;
this is what the king's law must punish.
King Wèiliè not only failed to punish them,
he further appointed them as feudal lords,
this was to honor and reward ministers who were treacherous, usurped names, and transgressed their proper stations.
The Comprehensive Mirror begins here,
is it not to emphasize the importance of names and stations!
Your subject Guāng says: Your subject has heard that the duty of the Son of Heaven is none greater than ritual,
ritual none greater than station,
station none greater than name.
What is called ritual?
It is the guiding principles.
What is called station?
It is ruler and minister.
What is called name?
It is duke, marquis, minister, and grand master.
Now, with the vastness of the realm within the four seas,
the multitude of the myriad people,
all controlled by one man,
even if one possesses peerless strength,
wisdom surpassing the age,
none
do not run to serve and perform duties,
is it not because ritual serves as the guiding principles
for this!
Therefore, the Son of Heaven commands the Three Dukes,
the Three Dukes lead the feudal lords,
the feudal lords control the ministers and grand masters,
the ministers and grand masters govern the officers and common people.
The noble oversee the base,
the base support the noble.
The superior employing the inferior is like the heart and belly operating the limbs,
the root and trunk controlling the branches and leaves;
the inferior serving the superior is like the limbs defending the heart and belly,
the branches and leaves sheltering the root and trunk.
Only then can superiors and inferiors mutually protect each other and the state be well-ordered and secure.
Therefore it is said: The duty of the Son of Heaven is none greater than ritual.
King Wén arranged the Yìjīng,
beginning with Qián and Kūn.
Confucius appended the commentary:
"Heaven is lofty, earth is lowly;
thus Qián and Kūn are established.
The lowly and the lofty are arrayed,
and the positions of the noble and the base are fixed."
This means the positions of ruler and minister are like heaven and earth and cannot be altered.
The Spring and Autumn Annals restrained the feudal lords
and honored the royal
house.
Even though the king's men were of low rank,
they were placed above the feudal lords,
showing that the sage never neglected the relationship between ruler and minister.
Unless there was the tyranny of a Jié or Zhòu,
and the benevolence of a Tāng or Wǔ,
with the people turning to them
and Heaven's Mandate bestowed upon them,
the distinction between ruler and minister should be maintained, and one should preserve integrity and accept death.
Thus, if Wēizǐ had replaced Zhòu, then Chéng Tāng would have been matched with Heaven.
Historical Records: The Shāng emperor Dì Yǐ had three sons: the eldest was Wēizǐ Qǐ,
the second was Zhòng Yǎn,
and the youngest was Zhòu.
Zhòu's mother was the empress.
Dì Yǐ wished to establish Qǐ as crown prince,
but the Grand Historian, citing the law, protested:
"There is a son by the wife;
a son by a concubine cannot be established."
Thus Zhòu was established.
Zhòu ultimately brought about the fall of the Yīn state through his tyranny and cruelty.
Kǒng
[Zhèng]
likened the father to Heaven,
matching him with it;
in the practice of filial piety,
nothing is greater than this,
which is what is meant by
"Revering the father is nothing greater than matching him with Heaven."
Also, Kǒng said: The Lǐjì states that all things originate from Heaven,
and humans originate from ancestors.
Since both are origins,
they can be matched;
therefore, kings all match their ancestors with Heaven.
The rules of posthumous names: "Eliminating the cruel and removing the oppressive is called Tāng."
However, the rules of posthumous names originated in the Zhōu;
it seems the Yīn people had this title first,
and the Zhōu people later adopted it into the rules of posthumous names.
Fēn,
read as fú wèn fān.
Zhǎng,
read as zhī liǎng fān.
Zú,
read as zǐ xù fān.
If Jì Zhá had become ruler of Wú, then Tàibó would have received sacrificial offerings.
King Shòumèng of Wú had four sons: the eldest was Zhūfán,
the second was Yúzhài,
the third was Yúmèi,
and the youngest was Jì Zhá.
Jì Zhá was virtuous,
and Shòumèng wished to establish him,
but Jì Zhá declined and refused,
so Zhūfán was established.
When Zhūfán died,
he passed it to Yúzhài,
intending that the brothers pass it on in order,
eventually reaching Jì Zhá;
but Jì Zhá ultimately declined and fled.
Later, Zhūfán's son Guāng and Yúmèi's son Liáo contended for the state,
leading to Fūchāi,
and Wú consequently perished.
Ancestral temple sacrifices used livestock,
hence "blood offerings."
Tàibó
was the founding ruler of Wú.
Fàn Nìng said: Tài
is an honorific for greatness;
Bó
means eldest.
He was the first son of King Tàiwáng of Zhōu,
hence called Tàibó.
Lù Dé Míng said: Shòumèng,
read as mò gōng fān.
Yúzhài,
read as cè jiè fān.
Yúmèi,
read as mò.
Truly, the great principles of ritual cannot be disordered.
Therefore it is said: Nothing in ritual is greater than distinction.
Ritual
distinguishes noble and base,
orders closeness and distance,
regulates all things,
governs various affairs;
without names, they are not manifest,
without vessels, they are not embodied;
names are used to designate them,
vessels are used to differentiate them,
only then do high and low become clearly ordered,
this is the great principle of ritual.
Once names and vessels are lost,
how can ritual alone remain!
In the past, Zhòng Shū Yúxī had merit for Wèi,
he declined a fief and requested a fányīng,
Confucius considered it better to give him more fiefs.
Only names and vessels
cannot be lent to others,
they are what the gentleman oversees;
if governance is lost, the state follows.
Zuǒzhuàn: Sūn Huánzǐ of Wèi led troops to battle with the Qí army at Xīnzhù,
the Wèi army was defeated.
Zhòng Shū Yúxī of Xīnzhù rescued Sūn Huánzǐ,
and Huánzǐ was thus spared.
Afterwards, the people of Wèi rewarded him with a fief,
which he declined;
he requested a qūxuán and fányīng for court appearances,
and it was granted.
Confucius heard of this and said:
"It would have been better to give him more fiefs.
Only names and vessels cannot be lent to others."
Fányīng
are horse trappings.
Fán
is an ornament on the horse's mane;
yīng
is an ornament on the horse's chest.
A note in the Jìnshū states: The yīng on the horse's chest is like a ribbon.
Fán,
read as pú guān fān.
Yīng,
read as yī yíng fān.
Suǒ,
read as xī gè fān.
Confucius wished first to rectify names,
believing that if names are not rectified, the people would not know where to put hand or foot.
See the Analects.
A small matter,
yet Confucius valued it;
rectifying names,
a minor task,
yet Confucius put it first:
truly because once names and vessels are disordered, high and low have nothing to rely on.
There is no affair that does not begin subtly and become manifest;
the sage's foresight is far-reaching,
thus he can carefully manage it while subtle,
while the multitude's understanding is near-sighted,
so they must wait until it is manifest before remedying it;
managing it while subtle requires little effort and yields great results,
remedying it once manifest exhausts strength and may not succeed.
The Yì says:
"Treading on frost, solid ice is near,"
the line statement for the first six of Kūn.
The Xiàng says:
"Treading on frost, solid ice,
is the beginning of yin's congealing.
Following its course,
leads to solid ice."
"One day, two days, ten thousand subtle signs,"
words from the Gāoyáo mó.
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary says: Jī,
means subtle.
It means one should be cautious and fearful of the subtle signs of all affairs.
Jī,
read as jū yī fān.
Therefore it is said: Nothing in distinction is greater than names.
Alas!
When King Yōu and King Lì lost their virtue,
the Way of Zhōu declined daily,
its laws and order scattered and ruined,
the lower usurping the upper and the high positions being abandoned,
the feudal lords launched campaigns on their own authority,
referring to the likes of Duke Huán of Qí, Duke Wén of Jìn down to Duke Dào, King Zhuāng of Chǔ, and Fūchāi of Wú.
They seized power in their states,
referring to the likes of the Six Ministers of Jìn, the Three Families of Lǔ, and the Tián clan of Qí.
Yet the sacrifices to King Wén and King Wǔ continued unbroken,
because the descendants of Zhōu were still able to uphold their titles and duties.
How can this be explained?
In the past, Duke Wén of Jìn performed great service for the royal house,
and requested the privilege of a "suì" burial from King Xiāng.
King Xiāng did not grant it,
saying:
"This is the regulation of the king.
Without a change in virtue, there cannot be two kings,
which is also what you, my uncle, would detest.
Otherwise,
if you, my uncle, have land and wish to use a suì,
why request it from me!"
Duke Wén then feared and did not dare to transgress.
During the rebellion of Prince Dài,
King Xiāng fled and resided at Fàn.
Duke Wén of Jìn led troops to escort the king back,
and killed Prince Dài.
After settling King Xiāng at Jiá,
the king offered him land as a reward,
but he declined;
he requested the suì privilege,
but the king did not grant it, and so on.
Dù Yù said: "Suì" means digging a passage underground;
this was the burial ritual of the king.
Feudal lords lowered their coffins by ropes.
"Regulation of the king"
means to clearly distinguish the king from the feudal lords.
In ancient times, the Son of Heaven addressed feudal lords of the same surname as uncles.
Suì,
pronounced suì.
Detest,
pronounced wù.
Rebellion,
pronounced nàn.
Fàn,
pronounced fàn.
Reward,
pronounced lào.
Dig,
pronounced quē.
Lower by rope,
pronounced xuán.
Coffin,
pronounced jiù.
In terms of population, Zhōu was no larger than Zhū or Jǔ,
Cáo, Téng, Zhū, and Jǔ
were small states during the Spring and Autumn period.
Jǔ,
pronounced jǔ.
Yet it presided over the world as the suzerain,
and even powerful states like Jìn, Chǔ, Qí, and Qín did not dare to encroach upon it.
Why?
Simply because its title and duty still remained.
As for the Jì clan in Lǔ,
Tián Cháng in Qí,
Lord Bái in Chǔ,
and Zhì Bó in Jìn,
the Jì clan, ministers of Lǔ,
from Jì Yǒu onward,
generations held the governance of Lǔ.
Jì Píngzǐ expelled Duke Zhāo,
and Jì Kāngzǐ expelled Duke Āi,
yet they remained subjects their whole lives,
not daring to usurp the state.
Tián Cháng
is Chén Héng.
The Tián clan originally was the Chén clan;
Sīmǎ Guāng avoided the imperial taboo
and changed
"Héng"
to
"Cháng".
Chén Chéngzǐ gained control of Qí's governance,
killed Kǎn Zhǐ,
assassinated Duke Jiǎn,
yet also did not dare to establish himself.
The Shǐjì "Hereditary Houses" records Chén Jìngzhòng Wán as Tián Jìngzhòng Wán,
and Chén Chéngzǐ Héng as Tián Cháng,
so the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn follows this as a basis.
Lord Bái Shèng killed the Chǔ Prime Minister Zǐxī and Minister of War Zǐqī,
Shí Qǐ said:
"Burn the treasury and kill the king,
otherwise we will not succeed!"
Lord Bái said:
"Killing the king is inauspicious,
burning the treasury leaves no resources."
Zhì Bó, during Jìn's decline,
monopolized its governance,
invaded neighboring states,
and was the strongest among Jìn's ministers;
he attacked Duke Chū of Jìn,
and Duke Chū died on the road.
Zhì Bó wished to annex Jìn but did not dare,
so he installed Duke Āi Jiāo as ruler.
Yet in the end, he did not dare.
Was it because his strength was insufficient or his heart was not ruthless enough?
It was because he feared that violating titles and duties would lead to the whole world jointly punishing him.
Now the ministers of Jìn violently scorned their ruler,
carved up the state of Jìn,
the Shǐjì "Chronological Table of the Six States" records: In the sixteenth year of King Dìng,
Zhào, Wèi, and Hán destroyed Zhì Bó,
and then divided the state of Jìn into three.
Moreover, they were honored and ranked,
and made to stand among the feudal lords.
This means that even that small title and duty could not be maintained and was completely abandoned.
The rites of the former kings were exhausted at this point!
Some may think that at that time,
the Zhōu house was weak,
and the Three Jìn were strong,
the three families divided the state of Jìn,
and at that time they were therefore called
"the Three Jìn",
like the later Three Qín and Three Qí.
How could it be otherwise!
This is greatly mistaken.
Although the Three Jìn were strong,
if they disregarded the punishment of the world and violated righteousness to encroach upon ritual,
then they would not have requested from the Son of Heaven but would have established themselves.
Not requesting from the Son of Heaven and establishing themselves,
then they would be rebellious ministers,
and if there were lords like Duke Huán or Duke Wén in the world,
they would surely uphold ritual and righteousness to campaign against them.
Now they requested from the Son of Heaven and the Son of Heaven permitted it,
so they received the mandate of the Son of Heaven and became feudal lords.
Who could then campaign against them!
Therefore, the Three Jìn standing among the feudal lords
was not the Three Jìn destroying ritual,
but the Son of Heaven destroying it himself.
Alas!
Once the rituals between ruler and minister were ruined,
the world contended for supremacy with cunning and strength,
causing the descendants of sages and worthies who were feudal lords
to have their altars of soil and grain completely extinguished,
referring to Qí and Sòng perishing to the Tián clan,
Lǔ, Chén, and Yuè perishing to Chǔ,
and Zhèng perishing to Hán.
Extinguished,
pronounced mǐn,
means completely gone,
also pronounced mín.
Máo Huǎng said: It means to perish,
to be destroyed.
Is this not sorrowful!
2 At the beginning,
Zhì Xuānzǐ intended to make Yáo his heir.
Zhì Guǒ said:
"He is not as good as Xiāo.
Wéi Zhāo said: Zhì Xuānzǐ was Shēn, son of the Jìn minister Xún Lì.
Yáo was Zhì Xuānzǐ's son, Zhì Bó,
posthumously titled Xiāngzǐ.
Zhì Guǒ was a member of the Zhì clan.
Xiāo was a son of Xuānzǐ by a concubine.
According to the rules for posthumous names: 'Sagely, good, and widely informed' is called 'Xuān'.
The Zhì clan bestowed this flattering name.
The first way in which he falls short.
Wéi Zhāo said: He is not benevolent.
In the popular copies of the Comprehensive Mirror, many write
"beautiful beard",
which is incorrect.
The Discourses of the States writes
"beautiful temples",
and we follow that now.
【Chapter: The twelve-line edition correctly writes
"temples";
the Kǒng edition is the same.
The B edition eleven-line edition writes
"beard".
Being fully accomplished in arts and skills is worthy,
being clever with words and eloquent in debate is worthy,
Wéi Zhāo said: 'Jǐ' means sufficient.
'Qiǎo wén' means clever with literary phrasing.
'Jì' is pronounced qí qǐ fān.
Being like this, yet extremely unbenevolent.
If he uses these five worthy qualities to oppress others and acts with unbenevolence,
who can tolerate him?
Wéi Zhāo said: 'Dài' means to tolerate.
The Zhì lineage will certainly be destroyed."
He did not listen.
Zhì Guǒ separated his lineage from the Grand Scribe,
becoming the Fǔ clan.
This event is seen in the Discourses of the States.
According to the Zuǒzhuàn, the 23rd year of Duke Āi,
Jìn's Xún Yáo attacked Qí,
first appearing in the tradition.
The 23rd year of Āi corresponds to the fifth year of King Yuán in the Historical Records.
Xún Lì was Zhì Wénzǐ.
In the 14th year of Dìng,
Zhì Wénzǐ still appears in the tradition.
As for the affairs of Zhì Xuānzǐ,
the tradition has nothing to verify them.
The proposal to establish Yáo
should have been before the fifth year of King Yuán.
Wéi Zhāo said: The Grand Scribe is in charge of clans and surnames,
a subordinate of the Spring Offices in the Rites of Zhōu;
the Lesser Scribe is in charge of determining genealogies,
distinguishing the zhāo-mù order.
Minister Zhèng Sīnóng's commentary states: Scribes are in charge of writing,
hence when Hán Xuānzǐ visited Lǔ,
he viewed the books at the Grand Scribe's.
'Shìxì' refers to things like the Imperial Genealogy and the Origins of the Generations;
the Lesser Scribe is in charge of determining them.
Jiǎ Gōngyàn's subcommentary says: The commentary cites the Grand Scribe to verify it because
the Grand Scribe is the head of the scribes,
and they share the duties.
Probably according to the Zhōu system,
the Lesser Scribe determined surnames and clans,
but the records were held by the Grand Scribe.
Zhì Guǒ wished to avoid the disaster of the Zhì clan,
so he separated his lineage at the Grand Scribe's.
Sòng Qí's Supplementary Pronunciations for the Discourses of the States: 'Bié' is pronounced bié liè fān;
also read as the usual pronunciation.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ's sons,
the elder was called Bólǔ,
the younger was called Wúxù.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ was Yāng, grandson of Wénzǐ.
Rules for posthumous names: 'Unwavering in single virtue' is called 'Jiǎn'.
The White Tiger Discourse says: 'Zǐ' means to multiply,
multiplying without cease.
Zhào Qí said: 'Zǐ' is a general term for men.
'Zhǎng' is pronounced zhī liǎng fān.
Not knowing which to establish,
he then wrote admonitory words on two bamboo slips,
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: 'Shū' means to express.
The Shūwěi Xuánjīqián says: 'Shū' means 'like'.
Thus, 'shū' means to write down words as they express the meaning,
allowing them to be expressed and extended.
Origins of the Generations says: Jǔ Sòng and Cāng Jié created writing.
Explaining it,
[it is called]
'shù' also,
recording the multitude of things;
also called 'zhù',
writing it on slips and paper,
seeking not to perish.
'Jiǎn' are bamboo slips.
He gave them to his two sons, saying:
"Carefully remember them!"
After three years he asked them,
Bólǔ could not recite the words;
when asked for his slip,
he had already lost it.
Asking Wúxù,
he recited the words very fluently;
'xí' means proficient.
He took it from his sleeve and presented it.
Máo Huàng said: 'Zòu' means to present to a superior.
He was established as the heir.
Jiǎnzǐ sent Yǐn Duó to govern Jìnyáng.
The Surname Compendium: The surname Yǐn comes from a son of Shǎohào,
enfeoffed at Yǐn City,
his descendants thus took it as their clan name.
Wéi Zhāo said: Jìnyáng was a city of the Zhào clan.
'Wéi' means to govern.
Bān's Treatise says: Jìnyáng was the ancient Táng state of the Odes.
King Chéng of Zhōu destroyed Táng,
and enfeoffed his younger brother Shū Yú there.
Lóng Mountain is to the west,
from where the Jìn River flows out,
entering the Fén River to the east.
Minister Zàn said: The so-called Táng
is present-day Yǒng'ān County in Hédōng,
four hundred lǐ from Jìn.
The Expanded Geography Records says: The old city of Jìnyáng,
now called Jìn City,
is west of Yúxiāng County in Pú Prefecture.
Now, according to the Commentary on the Water Classic: The Jìn River flows out from Lóng Mountain west of Jìnyáng County.

1 There was a solar eclipse.
Dù Yù states: the sun moves slowly,
completing one circuit of the heavens in a year.
The moon moves quickly,
completing one circuit in a month;
thus, they intersect twelve times a year.
However, the sun and moon,
as moving bodies,
though their paths are largely regular,
cannot avoid slight variations,
so there are times when they intersect without an eclipse,
or times when frequent intersections cause eclipses.
Kǒng Yǐngdá states: the intersection of the sun and moon
refers to the new moon.
A circuit of the heavens is 365 and 1/4 degrees.
Both the sun and moon move rightward across the heavens;
in one day and night,
the sun moves one degree,
while the moon moves 13 and 7/19 degrees.
After 29 days, with some remainder,
the moon completes a circuit of the heavens
and catches up to the sun, intersecting with it.
If the intersection occurs while both are on the same path, an eclipse occurs;
if the moon is either north or south of the sun's path,
no eclipse occurs.
Additionally, astronomers calculate eclipse cycles,
generally using a limit of about 173 days.
However, if the moon is initially south of the sun's path,
eclipses within the limit are more frequent;
if the moon is north of the sun's path,
eclipses within the limit are less frequent.
Dù Yù observed these irregularities
and stated
"though their paths are largely regular,
they cannot avoid slight variations,
so there are times when they intersect without an eclipse,
or times when frequent intersections cause eclipses,"
which is accurate.
Sū Shì states: when intersection occurs at the new moon, a solar eclipse may happen,
but there are also intersections without eclipses.
An eclipse during intersection
occurs when yáng is weak and yīn overpowers it;
no eclipse during intersection
occurs when yáng is strong and yīn cannot obscure it.
Zhū Yuánhuī states: this relates to human affairs.
When ministers betray their rulers,
wives overpower their husbands,
petty men oppress gentlemen,
or barbarians invade the Central States,
such influences
cause yīn to overpower yáng, resulting in a solar eclipse.
Thus, in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the Sage recorded every eclipse,
and poets also regarded them as inauspicious.
Here, the year is recorded but not the month or the day of the new moon,
which is an omission by the historian.
Shìmíng states: the waning of the sun or moon is called an eclipse;
a gradual encroachment,

Following the *Biographies* and the *Strategies of the Warring States*,

This follows what is recorded in the chronological tables and hereditary houses.
Probably because the *Biographies of Assassins* initially does not mention also killing Marquis Āi,
only the *Strategies of the Warring States* mentions it,
could it be that the *Comprehensive Mirror* doubted this!

At this time, east of the Hé and Shān were six powerful states.
The Hé River, from its upper mouth at Lóngmén,
flows south to Huáyīn and then east;
the Qín state was west of the Hé.
The Shān mountains, from Niǎoshǔtóngxué, extend continuously as the Cháng'ān Southern Mountains,
reaching Tàihuà;
the Qín state was west of the Shān.
The six states of Hán, Wèi, Zhào, Qí, Chǔ, and Yān were all east of the Hé and Shān.
Huá,
hù huà fān.
Yān,
yīn jiān fān.
In Nányáng Commandery, southeast of Píngshì County are the Tóngbǎi and Dàfù Mountains,
source of the Huái River,

The Sì River originates southwest of Biàn County in the Lǔ state,

The states of Sòng, Lǔ, Zōu, Téng, Xuē, and Ní,

As King Wēi of Qí said,
"the twelve lords of Sìshàng."
Wèi built a long wall,
from Zhèng along the Luò northwards, possessing the Shàng Commandery;
Zhèng County,

Luò,

from Zhèng along the Luò."
Sòng Bái says: Present-day east of Huá Prefecture is Wèi's long wall.
The Shàng Commandery,
belonged to Bìng Province in Hàn times,
Suí and Táng's Suí Prefecture and Yán Prefecture,

Bīn,
pronounced bīn.

Qián,
qú jīn fān.
Dí,

Thereupon, Duke Xiào, stirred with indignation,
spread virtue and improved governance,
desiring to strengthen Qín.
1 Duke Xiào issued an order to the state, saying:
"In the past, our Duke Mù,
from between Qí and Yōng cultivated virtue and practiced military arts,
pacified the chaos in Jìn to the east,
taking the river as the boundary,
dominated the Róng and Dí tribes to the west,
expanded the territory for a thousand lǐ,
the Son of Heaven conferred the title of Bó,
the feudal lords all came to congratulate,
opening a foundation for later generations that was very glorious and splendid.
But in the times of the past Dukes Lì, Zào, Jiǎn, and Chūzǐ, there was unrest,
the state faced internal worries,
and had no leisure for external affairs.
The three states of Jìn attacked and seized the lands west of the river from our former rulers,
a shame of the utmost magnitude.
When Duke Xiàn ascended the throne,
he pacified and guarded the borders,
moved the capital to Yuèyáng.
Shǐjì: In the second year of Duke Xiàn of Qín,
he began to rule from Yuèyáng.
Xú Guǎng's annotation says: That is the Hàn dynasty's Wànnián County.
I note that according to the Hànshū,
Yuèyáng and Wànnián were two separate counties,
both belonging to Féngyì,
and it was only in the Later Hàn that they were merged.
Sòng Bái says: Yuèyáng,
was an old Qín county.

he still divided Yuèyáng to establish Wànnián County as the mausoleum town,
administering it within the walls of Yuèyáng city,
thus Yuèyáng city was also called Wànnián city.
In the Later Hàn, Yuèyáng County was abolished and merged into Wànnián County.
During the Dàtǒng era of the Later Wèi,
Wànnián was divided to establish Zhāngqiū and Xuānwǔ,
and also divided to establish Guǎngyáng County.
Emperor Míng of Zhōu abolished Wànnián and merged it into Gāolíng and Guǎngyáng counties,
and instead established Wànnián County separately within the city of Cháng'ān.
In the first year of the Wǔdé era of Táng,
Guǎngyáng was again changed to Yuèyáng,
and in the fifteenth year of the Yuánhé era,
it was transferred and attached to Fèngxiān County to serve the Jǐnglíng Mausoleum.
Yuè, pronounced yào.
He recovered the former territories of Duke Mù,
and restored Duke Mù's governance and decrees.
I, the unworthy one, think upon the intentions of our former rulers,
and it often pains my heart.
If among the guests and ministers there is anyone who can devise extraordinary plans to strengthen Qín,
I will honor him with high office,
and share the land with him."
Meaning to divide the land to enfeoff him,
so that each would have a share of territory.
Fēn,
pronounced fù wèn fān.
Then he went west into Qín.
Gōngsūn Yāng,
was a collateral descendant of Wèi,
and was fond of the studies of xíngmíng.
Yán Shìgǔ says: Liú Xiàng's Biélù states: Master Shēn's learning favored xíngmíng.
Xíngmíng means,
following names to demand substance,
its honoring the ruler and debasing the ministers,
elevating the superior and suppressing the inferior,
accords with the Six Classics.
Some commentators say: Xíng,
the School of Punishment;
míng,
the School of Names;
these are two of the six schools discussed by Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān.
This interpretation is incorrect.
Liú Yuánfù says: Xíngmíng,
means studying the techniques of both schools together.
Gōngsūn is not a surname,
because his ancestors came from Wèi,
if his father was a ruler of Wèi he would be called Gōngzǐ,
if his grandfather was a ruler of Wèi he would be called Gōngsūn.
Yāng,
pronounced yú liǎng fān.
Cuó knew he was worthy,
but had not yet recommended him.
Then he fell ill,
and King Huì of Wèi went to visit him and asked:
"If your illness, Gōngshū, should prove
incurable,
what will become of the altars of soil and grain?"
Gōngshū said:
"Among my attendants is Wèi Yāng,
since the Warring States period,
the households of senior officials have had zhōngshùzǐ,
and shèrén.
He has extraordinary talent,
I wish you would entrust the entire state to him and heed his counsel!"
The king remained silent.
Gōngshū said:
"If you, my lord, do not heed and employ Yāng,
you must kill him,
do not let him leave the state!"
The king promised and left.
Gōngshū summoned Yāng and apologized, saying:
"I put my ruler first and my minister second,
xiān, hòu,
both pronounced in the departing tone.
Later I told you.
These xiān, hòu,
are both pronounced as usual.
Wèi,
pronounced yú wèi fān.
Yāng said:
"Since my lord did not use your words to employ me,
how could he use your words to kill me!"
In the end, he did not leave.
The king, after leaving,
said to his attendants:
"Gōngshū is gravely ill,
how pitiful,
he wanted me to entrust the state to Wèi Yāng!
Then he also urged me to kill him,
is that not perverse!"
After Wèi Yāng arrived in Qín,
through the favored minister Jǐng Jiàn he sought an audience with Duke Xiào,
and persuaded him with methods to enrich the state and strengthen the military;
the duke was greatly pleased,
and discussed state affairs with him.
1. Wèi Yāng wished to reform the laws,
but the people of Qín were displeased.
Wèi Yāng addressed Duke Xiào of Qín, saying:
"The common people cannot be consulted at the beginning of an enterprise,
but they can share in its successful completion.
Those who discuss the highest virtue do not conform to popular customs;
those who achieve great merit do not seek counsel from the multitude.
Therefore, if a sage can strengthen the state,
he does not adhere to old precedents."
Suǒyǐn says: This means the method of governance to remedy defects;
if the actions taken can strengthen the state,
then it is not necessary to follow old precedents.
"Otherwise,
Suǒyǐn says: Gān,
a surname;
Lóng,
a given name.
The surname Gān originated from Prince Dài of Gānzhāo during the Spring and Autumn period.
The Xìngpǔ also says: The surname Gān
descends from Gān Pán of the Shāng dynasty.
Officials become accustomed to it, and the people feel at ease with it."
Wèi Yāng said:
"Ordinary people are content with old customs;
scholars are immersed in what they have heard.
With these two types of people,
one can occupy office and uphold the law,
but they are not fit to discuss matters beyond the law.
The wise create laws;
the foolish are bound by them.
The worthy revise rites;
the unworthy are constrained by them."
The Duke said:
"Good."
He appointed Wèi Yāng as Zuǒ Shùzhǎng.
Liú Shào's Juézhì says: The Zuǒzhuàn mentions a Shùzhǎng Bào.
When Lord Shāng administered the government,
he established a system of eighteen ranks;
including Guānnèihóu and Lièhóu,
there were twenty grades in total.
This system was based on ancient principles.
In ancient times, the Son of Heaven entrusted military administration to the Six Ministers;
in peacetime they managed fields,
in times of alarm they fought in war,
which is what is meant by
"inwardly they govern,
outwardly they lead,
those long trusted achieve harmony with the masses"
Thus, when Qǐ attacked the Yǒuhù,
he summoned the Six Ministers,
who were the great officers serving as generals in the army.
By the Zhōu dynasty's Six Ministers,
they also resided with the army.
In the state,
they were called Bǐzhǎng, Lǘxū, Zúshī, Dǎng, Zhōuzhǎng, Qīng Dàfū;
in the army,
they were designated as Sīmǎ, Jiāngjūn, Zú, Wǔ,
to distinguish them from their titles in the state.
Qín followed the ancient system;
in the army, ranks were bestowed as grades,
and the soldiers were all Gēngzú.
Those who merited rank by achievement
were then included among the military officers.
From the first grade up to Bùgēng,
four grades,
were all Shì.
From Dàfū up to Wǔdàfū,
five grades,
corresponded to Dàfū.
Nine grades,
followed the principle of the nine bestowals.
From Zuǒ Shùzhǎng to Dà Shùzhǎng,
corresponded to the Nine Ministers.
Guānnèihóu
followed the ancient principle of Zǐ and Nán within the royal domain.
The Qín capital was west of the mountains,
considering the area within the passes as the royal domain,
hence called Guānnèihóu.
Lièhóu
followed the ancient principle of feudal lords of separate states.
Thus, the grades below Qīng, Dàfū, and Shì
all imitated the ancient court system but differed in name,
also to distinguish between military and state affairs.
In ancient times, chariots were used in warfare;
one war chariot,
with seventy-two infantrymen,
divided into wings left and right;
on the chariot,
the Dàfū was on the left,
the driver in the center,
a warrior on the right,
totaling seventy-five men.
The first rank, called Gōngshì,
was for infantrymen who held the rank of Gōngshì.
The second rank, called Shàngzào,
Zào,
means completion,
in ancient times, a Shì who completed training and was promoted by the Sītú was called Zàoshì;
though following this name,
they were all infantrymen.
The third rank, called Zānniǎo,
were drivers of four-horse chariots.
Yāoniǎo,
was a famous horse breed in ancient times;
driving a four-horse chariot,
its shape resembled a hairpin,
hence called Zānniǎo.
The fourth rank, called Bùgēng,
Bùgēng means
serving as the chariot right,
no longer the same as ordinary Gēngzú.
The fifth rank, called Dàfū,
was the Dàfū on the left of the chariot.
The sixth rank was Guāndàfū,
the seventh rank was Gōngdàfū,
the eighth rank was Gōngchéng,
the ninth rank was Wǔdàfū,
all were military officers.
The rank of officials and commoners could not exceed Gōngchéng;
it could be transferred to sons or brothers.
Thus, Gōngchéng
was the highest rank among military officers;
even if not in battle,
they could ride in a Gōngchéng carriage,
hence called Gōngchéng.
The tenth rank was Zuǒ Shùzhǎng,
the eleventh rank was Yòu Shùzhǎng,
the twelfth rank was Zuǒgēng,
the thirteenth rank was Zhōnggēng,
the fourteenth rank was Yòugēng,
the fifteenth rank was Shǎoshàngzào,
the sixteenth rank was Dàshàngzào,
the seventeenth rank was Sìchē Shùzhǎng,
the eighteenth rank was Dà Shùzhǎng,
the nineteenth rank was Guānnèihóu,
the twentieth rank was Lièhóu.
From Zuǒ Shùzhǎng to Dà Shùzhǎng,
all were Qīng and Dàfū,
all were military commanders;
those they commanded were all commoners and Gēngzú,
hence the names
"Shù"
and
"Gēng"
were used.
Dà Shùzhǎng
was the Grand General;
Zuǒ and Yòu Shùzhǎng
were the Left and Right Lieutenant Generals.
Zhǎng,
read as zhàng.
He ordered the people to be organized into groups of ten and five for mutual surveillance and collective responsibility.
Suǒyǐn says: Shōusī
means mutual exposure.
If one family committed a crime,
the other nine families would jointly report it;
if they did not report,
then all nine families would be held collectively responsible.
Shī Gǔ says: Five men formed a Wǔ,
two Wǔ formed a Shí.
Kāng says: Sī
means to manage.
The system of Shí and Wǔ
made them supervise and manage each other.
Qín had the law of witnessing and collective responsibility.
I say collective responsibility means
if one family was guilty,
the entire Shí and Wǔ would be held collectively responsible;

Zú,
read as zú.
Suǒyǐn says: Reporting one criminal would earn one rank,

Suǒyǐn says: The law: Those who surrender to the enemy are executed,
and their families are confiscated.
Now, concealing a criminal
means they should receive the same punishment.
Xiáng,
read as xiáng.
Each would receive higher rank according to the rate;
those who engaged in private fights
would be punished according to the severity of their offense.
They were to exert themselves in fundamental occupations;
those who farmed and wove, producing much grain and cloth,

those who pursued secondary profits or were idle and poor

Suǒyǐn says: Secondary profits
refer to crafts and trade.
They were exposed and their wives and children were registered,
confiscated as slaves.
Under Qín law,
if one person was guilty,
their household was confiscated.
By the first year of Emperor Wén of Hàn,

Nú,
read as nú.
Lùn,
means to deliberate.
There are military achievements that can be discussed.
Discuss,
Lú kùn fān,
Kāng Lú Kūn qiē.
Shǔ jí,
the register of the imperial clan.

The official Xiǎo Shǐ in the Zhōu Lǐ,
was in charge of determining the imperial lineage and genealogical records,
to understand the generations and order of precedence.
Shǔ,
shū yù fān.
Each according to their rank and order.
Báihǔ Tōng says: Jue (rank),
means to exhaust,

Máo Huǎng said: Officials above the rank of Dàfū participate in feasts and banquets,

Zhì (salary),
means duty,
office,
accumulation,
order,
constancy,
sequence.
Those with merit are honored and glorified,

The laws were already prepared but not yet promulgated,

a three-zhàng tall wooden pole was erected at the southern gate of the capital’s market,

One person moved it,
and was promptly given fifty jīn.
Lǐ Yún said: One jīn is a cube of gold one cùn on each side, weighing one jīn.
This is one jīn.
Chéng Dàchāng’s Yǎnfánlù says: Twenty liǎng is one jīn,
also called one yì.
After the laws were enforced for a full year,
the people of Qín who went to the capital
zhī,
means to go,
or to proceed.
At this time, the crown prince violated the law.
Wèi Yāng said:
“If the laws are not upheld,
it is because those above violate them.
The crown prince,
is the heir to the ruler.
He cannot be punished.”
So his tutor, Gōngzǐ Qián, was punished,
and his teacher, Gōngsūn Gǔ, was tattooed.
Tattooing the face with ink is called qíng.
Qíng,
pronounced qú jīng fān.
This sets the stage for Qín later killing Shāngjūn Yāng.
The people of Qín all hastened to obey the laws.
After ten years of enforcement,
in the state of Qín, no one picked up lost items on the road,
there were no bandits in the mountains,
the people were brave in public warfare,
but timid in private fights,
and the villages and towns were greatly well-governed.
From this year until the thirty-first year when Shāng Yāng died,
it seems that Yāng’s implementation of his laws and their effectiveness occurred within ten years,
and another ten years later brought disaster.
Zhì,
zhí lì fān.
Some came to say the laws were beneficial.
Wèi Yāng said:
“These are all people who disrupt the laws!”
He relocated all of them to the border.
After that, no one dared to discuss the laws.
Minister Guāng says: Trust,
is a great treasure for a ruler.
The state is preserved by the people,
the people are preserved by trust;
without trust, one cannot command the people,
without the people, one cannot defend the state.
Therefore, the ancient kings did not deceive the four seas,
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: From the present looking back to the past is called ancient.
Those skilled at governing a state do not deceive their people,
those skilled at managing a family do not deceive their relatives.
The unskilled do the opposite,
deceiving their neighboring states,
deceiving their people,
and even deceiving their brothers,
deceiving their fathers and sons.
If the superiors do not trust the subordinates,
and the subordinates do not trust the superiors,
then superiors and subordinates become estranged,
leading to defeat.
The gains cannot remedy the injuries,
the acquisitions cannot compensate for the losses,
is this not lamentable!
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí did not break his covenant with Cáo Mò,
Duke Wén of Jìn did not covet the profit of attacking Yuán,
Marquis Wén of Wèi did not abandon his appointment with the gamekeeper.
Xìngpǔ: The Cáo surname originated from Lù Zhōng, the great-great-grandson of Zhuānxū, whose sixth son Ān,
was the founder of the Cáo surname.
King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed Cáo Xiá at Zhū,

It also says: Cáo,
descended from Shū Zhènduó,
the younger brother of King Wǔ by the same mother,
later taken as a surname.
Shǐjì: Duke Huán of Qí attacked Lǔ,
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ requested peace,
Duke Huán agreed,
and they made a covenant at Kē.
As they were about to swear the covenant,
Cáo Mò held a dagger against Duke Huán on the altar,

Duke Huán agreed,
and Cáo Mò put down the dagger and returned to his minister’s position.

and wanted to kill Cáo Mò,

When the feudal lords heard of this,
they all trusted Qí and wished to submit to it.

he ordered the troops to withdraw.
A spy came out,
saying:
“Yuán is about to surrender.”
The military officers said:
“Please wait.”
The Duke said:
“To gain Yuán but lose trust,
the loss would be greater.”
They retreated thirty lǐ, and Yuán surrendered.
The affair of Marquis Wén of Wèi is seen in the twenty-third year of King Wèiliè in the previous volume.
Bèi,
pú mèi fān.
Suǒyǐn says: Mò,
pronounced wáng gě fān.
Zuǒzhuàn and Gǔliáng both write
“Cáo Guì.”
Thus, Mò should be pronounced Guì,
Mò and Guì have similar sounds but different characters.
These four rulers were not purely virtuous,
and Shāngjūn was especially known for harshness,
yet they lived in an age of warfare,
when the world tended toward deceit and force,
and still they did not dare to forget trust in order to nurture their people,
how much more should those who govern the four seas in times of peace and order!
2 Marquis Yì of Hán passed away,
and his son, Marquis Zhāo, succeeded him.
The rules of posthumous naming say: Zhāo means having virtue and toil is called Zhāo;

Qín used this as a pretext to lure and entrap his father,
while Qí took advantage of his father's departure to pressure him with benefits.
1 There was a solar eclipse,
total.
2 The people of Qín captured Ráng from Hán.
According to the Treatise of the Bān family,
Ráng County belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Based on the time period,
it should have belonged to Chǔ.
However, Hán had obtained the territory of Yǐngchuān,
which bordered Nányáng.
During the military conflicts among the Seven States,
the borders
shifted back and forth,
so perhaps Ráng belonged to Hán at this time?
Ráng,
pronunciation: rén yáng fān.
3 The Governor of Shǔ, Huī, rebelled against Qín,
and Qín's Sīmǎ Cuò went to execute him.
The Governor of Shǔ
refers to the governor of Shǔ Commandery.
The Qín Annals in the Records of the Grand Historian states
"the Marquis of Shǔ."
The Chronicles of Huáyáng states: Qín enfeoffed Prince Huī as the Marquis of Shǔ.
The Marquis of Shǔ performed a sacrifice,
and presented the sacrificial meat to the King;
his stepmother resented him,
and added poison to it before offering it.
The King was greatly enraged,
and sent Sīmǎ Cuò to bestow a sword upon Huī.
Shǒu (Governor),
pronunciation: shòu.
Huī,
the Suǒyǐn gives the pronunciation as huī.
4 The Qín Shùzhǎng Huàn joined forces with the armies of Hán, Wèi, and Qí to attack Chǔ,
to avenge the grudge over the Chǔ Crown Prince's escape and return.
Zhǎng,
pronunciation: zhī zhàng fān.
They killed its general Táng Miè;
and subsequently captured Zhòngqiū.
The surname Táng originates from Táng Yáo.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
there were two places named Zhòngqiū: When Wèi's Sūn Kuǎi watered his horses at Zhòngqiū,
Dù Yù said: It was a city of Cáo;
when the feudal lords formed an alliance at Zhòngqiū,
Dù Yù said: It was territory of Qí.
At this time, Chǔ's borders did not extend to either of these places.
The Annals of Lǚ Bùwéi states: Qí ordered Zhāngzǐ to attack Jīng (Chǔ) together with Hán and Wèi,
Jīng sent Táng Miè to lead troops in response,
and they encamped on opposite banks of the Cǐ River;
Zhāngzǐ attacked them at night,
and beheaded Miè on this river.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Cǐ River flows further west,
and the Ào River flows into it.
The Ào River originates north from the Zīqiū Mountains,
and flows south into the Cǐ River.
It is likely that Zhòngqiū is Zīqiū.
Bà (defeat),
pronunciation: bǔ mài fān.
Jiàng (general),
pronunciation: jí liàng fān.
"Miè",
in the Xúnzǐ is written as
"Miè",
Yáng Liàng's commentary states: It is the same as
"Miè"
the pronunciations are similar,
it should be pronounced as mò.
The Suǒyǐn gives the pronunciation as mò gé fān.
Zhòng,
pronunciation: zhí lóng fān.
Zī,
pronunciation: cái zhī fān.
5 The King of Zhào attacked Zhōngshān,
and the Lord of Zhōngshān fled to Qí.
1 The Qín Lord of Jīngyáng became a hostage in Qí.
2 The Qín Lord of Huáyáng attacked Chǔ,
greatly defeated the Chǔ army,
beheaded thirty thousand,
killed its general Jǐng Quē,
and captured Chǔ's Xiāngchéng.
According to the Treatise of the Bān family,
Xiāngchéng County belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery,
and had Xī Bùláng,
which is what King Líng of Chǔ referred to when he said
"the great cities of Chén, Cài, and Bùláng,
each can provide a thousand chariots in tax"
Jiàng (general),
pronunciation: jí liàng fān.
Lù Démíng said: Bùláng,
the old pronunciation is láng;
the Treatise on Geography in the Book of Hàn writes it as
"Gēng"
Shèng (chariot),
pronunciation: shéng zhèng fān.
He sent the Crown Prince to become a hostage in Qí to request peace.
This sets the stage for King Huái of Chǔ entering Qín and dying there, and Qí detaining the Crown Prince to coerce Chǔ.
3 Qín's Chūlǐjí died,
and the man from Zhào, Lóu Huǎn, was appointed as Chancellor.
4 King Wǔlíng of Zhào loved his younger son Hé,
and wished to establish him as heir while he (the King) was still alive.
1 On the Wùshēn day of the fifth month,
he held a grand court assembly at the Eastern Palace,
and transferred the state to Hé.
After the King completed the temple audience rites,
he came out to preside over the court.
Miào jiàn (temple audience),
refers to the first audience at the ancestral temple upon ascending the throne.
Jiàn (see),
pronunciation: xián biàn fān.
Féi Yì became the Xiànguó (Chancellor of State),
and also served as Tutor to the King.
The office of Xiànguó began here,
and Qín and Hàn followed it;
from Hàn and Wèi onwards,
its status and prestige were higher than that of Chéngxiàng (Chancellor).
Xiàng (Chancellor),
pronunciation: xī liàng fān.
"Zhǔfù" (Lord Father).
Zhǔfù,
means he is the father of the ruler of the state.
Another interpretation says,
it means his son rules the state while he himself is the father.
He himself wore Hú clothing,
and led the officers and gentlemen northwest to conquer Hú territory.
He planned to lead troops from Yúnzhōng and Jiǔyuán south to launch a surprise attack on Xiányáng.
Thereupon, he pretended to be an envoy himself,
and entered Qín,
wishing to observe Qín's terrain and the character of the King of Qín.
The King of Qín did not know,
but later was astonished by his exceptionally imposing appearance,
which was not the bearing of a subject.
After the host and guest had met,
and the rituals of interaction were completed,
he then became suspicious that he was not a subject.
By the time the Lord Father had already left and passed through the pass,
upon careful inquiry,
it turned out to be the Lord Father.
This means he had already slipped out of the Qín pass.
2 The King of Qí and the King of Wèi met in Hán.
3 The people of Qín attacked Chǔ,
and captured eight cities.
The King of Qín sent a letter to the King of Chǔ, saying:
"Initially, I, the humble one, made a covenant with you, Great King, to be as brothers,
and we swore an alliance at Huángjí,
see the eleventh year above.
Yí (send),
pronunciation: yú jì fān.
We were most cordial.
Your Crown Prince Líng killed my important minister,
and fled without offering apologies.
See the thirteenth year.
He sent troops to invade Your Majesty's borders.
Referring to the battle at Zhòngqiū,
and the capture of Xiāngchéng.
See the fifteenth year.
We are related by marriage and are close kin;
the father of the wife is called hūn,
the father of the son-in-law is called yīn.
According to character dictionaries: Hūn (marriage),
is hūn (dusk);
according to ritual, marriage takes place at dusk,
women are yīn (feminine principle),
hence it is called hūn.
The son-in-law's family is where the woman relies,
hence it is called yīn.
The Zìlín states: Hūn,
refers to the wife's family;
yīn,
refers to the son-in-law's family.
Jiǎ Gōngyàn said: Considering the individuals,
then the man is called hūn,
the woman is called yīn;
if considering the relatives,
then the woman's father is called hūn,
the son-in-law's father is called yīn.
In my opinion, Zhāng Yí said Qín and Chǔ marrying daughters and taking wives made them brotherly states;
examining the historical records,
from the fourth year of King Nǎn to this year,
Qín and Chǔ had not yet married or given in marriage.
In the nineteenth year,
King Huái of Chǔ died in Qín.
In the twenty-third year,
King Xiāng of Chǔ welcomed a wife from Qín.
It seems they had already agreed on the marriage alliance earlier,
and later, after King Xiāng completed the mourning period,
he then welcomed the wife to consummate the marriage.
Otherwise, I would have no way to command the feudal lords.
I, the humble one, wish to meet with you, Great King, at Wǔguān,
face to face to make an agreement,
swear an alliance, and then part,
this is my wish!"
The King of Chǔ was troubled by this.
If he went, he feared being deceived;
if he did not go, he feared Qín would grow even angrier.
Zhāo Suī said:
"Do not go, but instead mobilize troops to defend ourselves!
Qín is
a tiger and wolf,
with the intention of annexing the feudal lords;
it cannot be trusted!"
The King of Huái's son
Lán urged the king to go,
so the king entered Qín.
The King of Qín ordered a general to pretend to be the king,
ambushing troops at Wǔguān.
When the King of Chǔ arrived, they closed the pass and seized him,
taking him westward,
to Xiányáng,
where he was made to pay homage at Zhāngtái,
according to the rites for a vassal lord,
and pressured to cede the Wū and Qiánzhōng commanderies.
The King of Chǔ wanted to form an alliance,
but the King of Qín wanted to obtain the territory first.
The King of Chǔ angrily said:
"Qín deceived me,
and now forcefully demands territory from me!"
He therefore refused to agree.
The people of Qín detained him.
The great ministers of Chǔ were troubled by this,
and so conspired together, saying:
"Our king is in Qín and cannot return,
pressured to cede territory,
while the crown prince is held hostage in Qí;
if Qí and Qín conspire together,
then Chǔ will lose its state."
They wanted to establish one of the king's sons who was in the state.
Zhāo Suī said:
"Both the king and the crown prince are trapped among the feudal lords;
now to go against the king's command and establish his illegitimate son
is not appropriate!"
So they falsely announced to Qí
(the falsehood being
that the King of Chǔ had died and requesting the crown prince's return to rule Chǔ).
Someone said:
"It would be better to keep the crown prince to demand Chǔ's territory north of the Huái River."
The Chancellor of Qí said:
"That will not do!
If they establish a king in Yǐng,
(Yǐng was
the capital of Chǔ.
According to Bān Zhì: Jiānglíng County in Nánjùn
was the former Yǐng capital of Chǔ.
King Wén of Chǔ moved here from Dānyáng;
nine generations later,
King Píng fortified it;
ten more generations later,
Qín captured it,
and they moved east to Shòuchūn,
also naming it Yǐng.
The Shuǐjīng states: The Jiāng River flows east past the old southern wall of Jiānglíng County,
and further east past the southern wall of Yǐng City.
The commentary says: Present-day Jiānglíng City
was the site of the Chǔ shipyard,
the Zhǔgōng of the Spring and Autumn period.
Yǐng City is what Zǐ Náng, in his dying words, instructed to fortify.
Liú Xù said: The Yǐng City that was the old capital of Chǔ
is present-day Jìnán City, fifteen lǐ north of Jiānglíng County.)
Chancellor,
read as xiàng.
That person said:
"Not so.
If they establish a king in Yǐng,
we can then bargain with the new king, saying:
'Give me Lower Dōngguó,
and I will kill the crown prince for you.'
(Bargaining
means mutually demanding benefits,
like market dealings.
Give,
read as yǔ.
For,
read as wèi.)
We will then join with the three states to establish him."
(The three states
refer to Qí, Hán, and Wèi.)
The people of Chǔ established him.
4 The King of Qín, hearing of Lord Mèngcháng's worthiness,
sent Lord Jīngyáng as a hostage to Qí,
to request Lord Mèngcháng to come to Qín,
and the King of Qín made him chancellor.
1 Someone said to the King of Qín:
"If Lord Mèngcháng becomes chancellor of Qín,
he will certainly put Qí first and Qín second."
(First and second
are both read in the falling tone.)
The King of Qín then made Lóu Huǎn chancellor,
imprisoned Lord Mèngcháng,
and intended to kill him.
Lord Mèngcháng sent someone to seek help from the King of Qín's favored concubine.
The concubine said:
"I wish to have your lord's white fox fur robe."
(The white fox fur robe
is made by stitching together the fur from under the forelegs of foxes;
it is said that a robe worth a thousand gold is not made from the fur of a single fox.)
He had already presented it to the King of Qín,
and had nothing with which to meet the concubine's request.
Among his retainers was one skilled at dog-like theft,
who entered the Qín treasury,
stole the white fox fur robe, and presented it to the concubine.
The concubine then spoke on his behalf to the king, and he was released.
The king later regretted it,
and sent men to pursue him.
When Lord Mèngcháng reached the pass,
the pass law
was that guests could only leave at cockcrow.
At that time, it was still early.
(Early
is interchangeable with the ancient character for early.)
Among his retainers was one skilled at imitating a rooster's crow,
and upon hearing it, wild fowl all crowed.
Lord Mèngcháng was thus able to escape and return.
2 The people of Chǔ announced to Qín:
"Thanks to the spirits of the state altars,
our state has a king!"
The King of Qín was enraged,
dispatched troops out of Wǔguān to attack Chǔ,
beheaded fifty thousand, and captured sixteen cities.
3 The King of Zhào enfeoffed his younger brother
as Lord Píngyuán.
According to the "Treatise on Geography" in the Hànshū,
Píngyuán County belonged to Píngyuán Commandery.
Shèng was enfeoffed at Dōngwǔchéng,
and titled Lord Píngyuán,
meaning he was not enfeoffed at Píngyuán itself.
Dōngwǔchéng belonged to Qīnghé Commandery.
Dù Yòu said: This is present-day Wǔchéng County in Bèi Prefecture.
It seems that Dìngxiāng also had a place called Wǔchéng,
which at that time also belonged to Zhào,
therefore, to distinguish it,
"Dōng" (East)
was added here.
He maintained several thousand
retainers.
Among them was a man named Gōngsūn Lóng,
skilled in the sophistry of "hardness and whiteness" and "sameness and difference".
The "Treatise on Literature" in the Hànshū records: The Gōngsūn Lóngzǐ in fourteen chapters.
The commentary states: This is the person who engaged in the sophistry of "hardness and whiteness" and "sameness and difference".
Chéng Xuányīng's commentary on the Zhuāngzǐ states: Gōngsūn Lóng wrote the Shǒubái Lùn,
which circulated in the world.
"Hardness and whiteness"
is the same as "shǒubái",
meaning to stubbornly uphold his doctrine,
similar to the meaning of Mòzǐ's "Mòshǒu" (Mohist defense).
Since the theory of "hardness and whiteness" arose,
sophists have each held to their own right and wrong,
resulting in endless different doctrines.
Gōngsūn Lóng was able to unite the many differences into sameness,
hence it was called "sameness and difference".
A commentary to the Shǐjì states: The Tàikāng Geographical Records of Jìn says: In Xīpíng County of Rǔnán there was a Lóngyuān (Dragon Abyss),
whose water could be used to quench swords,
making them extremely hard and sharp.
Hence there was the theory of "hardness and whiteness" which said: Yellow
is the reason for hardness;
white
is the reason for sharpness.
Another version says: Yellow is the reason for not being hard,
white is the reason for not being sharp.
It is unknown which of these two theories is correct.
Shèng,
pronunciation shēng.
Cuì (quench),
pronunciation qǔnèi.
Kǒng Chuān traveled from Lǔ to Zhào.
According to the Kǒngcóngzǐ,
Kǒng Chuān
was a descendant of Confucius.
Sǔn Miǎn said: The surname Kǒng
originated from the descendants of King Tāng of Shāng.
Tracing back to Emperor Kù's consort Jiǎndí,
who swallowed a swallow's egg and gave birth to Qì.
He was granted the surname Zǐ.
By the time of Tāng,
because his ancestor was conceived by sensing a swallow (yǐ),
he was named Lǚ,
styled Tiānyǐ.
Later generations combined
"Zǐ"
with
"Yǐ",
thus beginning the surname Kǒng.
Later, in Sòng, Kǒngfù encountered the disaster caused by Huá Dū,
and his son fled to Lǔ,
therefore Confucius was born in Lǔ.
Miǎn,
pronunciation miǎnyǎn.
Kù,
pronunciation kǔwò.
Huá,
pronunciation hùhuà.
Nàn (disaster),
pronunciation nǎidàn.
"Three ears",
is like the saying in the Zhuāngzǐ about a chicken having three feet.
The Zhuāngzǐ commentary says numbers originate from one,
one and one make two,
two and one make three.
Although the name "three" is established,
in reality it has no fixed form.
Therefore, a chicken can be said to have three feet.
Similarly, two ears or three ears,
the theory is also like this.
Another explanation: The ear's function is hearing.
Two ears
is the physical form.
Considering hearing itself as well,
one can arrive at three.
Zāng,
as in zānghuò (male and female slaves).
Zānghuò
means male and female slaves.
Biàn (discriminate),
means to distinguish;
xī (analyze),
means to divide: meaning the distinctions are very subtle.
Shortly after, he took his leave and departed.
The next day, he again visited Lord Píngyuán.
Zǐgāo
was the courtesy name of Kǒng Chuān.
Fù (again),
pronunciation fúyòu.
"Yesterday, Gōngsūn's words were truly sophistical,
Máo Huǎng said: Chóu,
means formerly;
xī,
means evening;
chóuxī,
means yesterday evening.
He replied:
"Indeed.
He almost made Zāng have three ears.
Máo Huǎng said: Rán,
means 'like',
'yes',
a decisive word.
Jī (almost),
pronunciation jūyī.
Lìng (make),
means to cause,
pronunciation lìdīng.
But in reality it is wrong!
I would like to ask you, my lord: Now, to say 'three ears' is very difficult and actually false,
to say 'two ears' is very easy and actually true.
I wonder if you, my lord, will follow what is easy and true,
or will you also follow what is difficult and false?"
Lord Píngyuán had no reply.
The next day,
he said to Gōngsūn Lóng:
"Please do not debate with Kǒng Zǐgāo anymore!
Zōu Yǎn passed through Zhào.
Lord Píngyuán had him debate with Gōngsūn Lóng the theory that "a white horse is not a horse".
This is also the theory mentioned in the Zhuāngzǐ that "a dog is not a canine".
The commentary says: Dog and canine,
are one reality with two names. If name and reality correspond,
then this is a dog,
that is a canine.
If name and reality are separated,
then a dog is different from a canine.
Also, Mòzǐ said: A dog
is a canine.
However,
killing
killing
The main point is similar to the theory that a white horse is not a horse.
Zōu Zǐ said:
"It cannot be done.
The purpose of debate
is to distinguish different categories so they do not harm each other,
and to order different viewpoints so they do not cause confusion.
To express ideas and communicate intentions,
to clarify what is meant,
so that others may understand,
not to strive to confuse each other.
Therefore, the victor does not lose what he upholds,
and the vanquished gains what he seeks.
One debates to seek truth.
Even if one does not win the debate, one can still examine the truth,
which is called gaining what one seeks.
Therefore, debate can be engaged in.
But when it comes to using convoluted language to feign,
embellished words to deceive,
clever analogies to shift meanings,
leading people so they cannot grasp the intended meaning,
this harms the great Way.
To engage in petty, entangled
arguments and compete to have the last word,
cannot but harm a gentleman.
I, Yǎn, will not do this."
All present praised him.
Meaning everyone present praised Zōu Yǎn's words as good.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn records this
to show that petty sophistry ultimately cannot undermine the great Way.
Chù (reject),
pronunciation chìlǜ.
The Shuōwén says: Chù
means to demote or lower.
It can also be read the same as qū (bend).
