The Middle Reign of King Nǎn
1 King Huáiwáng of Chǔ fled to return home.
The people of Qín detected this,
and blocked the road to Chǔ.
(This means blocking his path back to Chǔ.)
Jiàn,
means a gap,
to travel via a path through a gap.
Jiàn,
pronounced as in ancient "xiàn".
Zǒu,
pronounced as "zòu",
also pronounced according to its usual reading.
The people of Zhào did not dare to receive him.
King Huáiwáng was about to flee to Wèi,
when the people of Qín caught up with him,
and took him back.
2 Duke Píng of Lǔ passed away,
and his son, Duke Mǐn, Jiǎ, succeeded him.
The Shìběn
records "Mǐn"
as
"Mǐn".
1 King Huáiwáng of Chǔ fell ill,
died in Qín,
and the people of Qín returned his body.
The people of Chǔ all pitied him,
mourning as if for a close relative.
The feudal lords henceforth did not regard Qín as righteous.
2 Qí, Hán, Wèi, Zhào, and Sòng jointly attacked Qín,
reaching Yánshì before turning back.
The Kuòdìzhì states: The old city of Yánshì,
also named Sīyánchéng,
is located in Ānyì County, Pǔzhōu.
It was the official in charge of the salt ponds,
hence called Yánshì.
Xú Guǎng said:
"Yán",
in one version is written as
"Jiān".
In the twelfth year,
Qín took Fēnglíng from Wèi,
and also took Wǔsuì from Hán.
Now, both were returned to make peace.
3 Lord Fù of Zhào toured the new territory,
(referring to the land newly taken from Zhōngshān by Zhào).
Xíng,
pronounced as "xià mèng fān".
He went west and met the King of Lóufán at Xīhé, securing his troops.
To the north of Zhào were the Róng tribes of Línhú and Lóufán.
Lóufán County in the Hàn Dynasty's Yànmén Commandery
was where the Lóufán Hú people resided.
Xīhé,
refers to the territory of the Hàn Dynasty's Xīhé Commandery.
4 King Xiāng of Wèi passed away,
and his son, King Zhāo, succeeded him.
The Shìběn says: King Zhāo,
was named Sù.
5 King Xiāng of Hán passed away,
and his son, King Xī, Jiù, succeeded him.
1 Qín's Commandant Cuò attacked Xiāngchéng of Wèi.
Commandant,
likely refers to the State Commandant.
According to Bān's records,
Xiāngchéng County belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery.
Considering the division of territories,
Yǐngchuān was within Hán's borders.
It seems Wèi and Hán shared the territory of Yǐngchuān,
and in their military struggles for dominance,
the borders
could change from Hán to Wèi overnight.
Thus, at this time, Xiāngchéng might have been Wèi's land,
which is plausible.
Yì,
pronounced as "yì".
2 Lord Fù of Zhào, together with Qí and Yān, destroyed Zhōngshān,
and relocated its king to Fūshī.
Upon returning,
he distributed rewards,
granted a great amnesty,
held a feast,
and allowed five days of public celebration.
3 Lord Fù of Zhào enfeoffed his eldest son Zhāng at Dài,
with the title Lord Ānyáng.
Lord Ānyáng was habitually extravagant,
and in his heart, he did not accept his younger brother.
(Meaning he did not accept his younger brother as king.)
Lǐ Duì said to Féi Yì:
"Young Master Zhāng is strong and ambitious,
with many followers and great desires.
Tián Bùlǐ is ruthless and arrogant.
These two together
are sure to have sinister plots.
When petty men have desires,
they think lightly and plan shallowly,
seeing only the benefits,
without regard for the harm.
Disaster is bound to come soon.
You bear heavy responsibilities and hold great power,
making you the starting point of disorder and the focus of calamity.
Why not claim illness, stay out of affairs, and hand over governance to Young Master Chéng,
so as not to become a step toward disaster?"
Tī,
means a step,
made of wood,
used for climbing.
Huòtī,
means a step leading to disaster.
Tī,
pronounced as "tiān lí fān".
Féi Yì said:
"Previously, Lord Fù entrusted the king to me,
saying: 'Do not change your principles,
nor alter your considerations.
Ér,
means you.
Carry this out for life!'
I bowed twice to receive the command and recorded it.
(Recording the king's command in the register.)
What greater change could there be!
The proverb says: 'If the dead were to return to life, the living should feel no shame.'
I wish to keep my word;
how can I also preserve my life?
You have offered me advice and shown loyalty.
However,
my word was given long ago,
and I dare not break it!"
Lǐ Duì said:
"Very well,
do your best!
I fear I will only see you until this year."
Yǐ,
means to stop,
meaning Féi Yì's life would end this year.
Lǐ Duì frequently visited Young Master Chéng to guard against Tián Bùlǐ.
(Frequent visits mean they conspired together to prepare.)
Shuò,
pronounced as "suǒ jiǎo fān".
Suǒyǐn says: This refers to Gāo Xìn mentioned below.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Xìn,
pronounced as "shēn";
Kāng says: pronounced as usual.
"Young Master Zhāng and Tián Bùlǐ appear friendly but are actually malicious.
They have support internally and commit violence externally.
(Having support means Zhāng is favored by Lord Fù.)
They would not hesitate to act.
Forging orders,
means forging Lord Fù's orders.
Lìng,
pronounced as "lì zhèng fān".
Dǎn,
pronounced as "shí zhàn fān".
They forget sleep at night,
and forget food when hungry.
We must be prepared against thieves.
(Meaning thieves are around Lord Fù, and we must be prepared against their movements.)
If the king is summoned, I must see him first;
I will put myself forward,
and only if there is no issue may the king enter."
Xìn Qī said:
"Good."
Lord Fù had King Huìwén face his ministers in court while he himself watched from the side.
Seeing his eldest son looking dejected,
turning north to serve as a minister,
yielding to his younger brother,
(yielding,
same as submitting.)
he then wanted to divide Zhào and make Prince Zhāng king in Dài.
The plan was not yet decided when it was halted.
Lord Fù and the king traveled to Shāqiū,
(Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Shāqiū is twenty lǐ northeast of Píngxiāng County in Xíng Prefecture.)
I note that Shāqiū Terrace
was built by Zhòu.
Bǎn Zhì states: Shāqiū is seventy lǐ northeast of Jùlù County in Jùlù Commandery.
They stayed in separate palaces.
(They) fraudulently summoned the king using Lord Fù’s order.
Féi Yì entered first,
and was killed.
Gāo Xìn immediately fought with the king.
(Gāo Xìn fought with the king and Prince Zhāng’s followers.)
The capital of Zhào was Hándān,
(coming from Hándān.)
(Hándān,
pronounced hán dān.)
(Resist,
same as oppose.)
(Difficulty,
pronounced nǎi dàn fān.)
Their faction was exterminated.
Prince Chéng became chancellor,
titled Ānpíng Jūn;
Lǐ Duì became Sīkòu.
(Sīkòu,
one of the six ministers of Zhōu,
in charge of punishments.)
Chéng and Duì monopolized governance.
When Prince Zhāng was defeated,
he fled to Lord Fù;
Lord Fù opened (the gate) for him.
(Meaning he opened the palace gate to let him in.)
(Flee,
pronounced zòu.)
Prince Zhāng died,
Chéng and Duì plotted:
“Because of Zhāng,
we besieged Lord Fù;
if we withdraw the troops now,
we will be exterminated!”
(Exterminate,
meaning execute,
destroy.)
They ordered:
“Anyone in the palace who comes out later will be executed!”
Everyone in the palace came out.
Lord Fù wanted to leave but could not,
and could not get food,
so he took fledgling birds and ate them.
(Ěryǎ says: Those fed by mouth,
are fledglings;
those that peck themselves,
are chicks.
Explanation: Distinguishing different names for young birds.
Young birds that need to be fed by the mother are fledglings,
such as swallows and sparrows.
Those that can peck food themselves are chicks,
such as chickens and pheasants.)
(Take,
pronounced tǔ nán fān.)
(Fledgling,
pronounced jū hòu fān.)
He starved to death in Shāqiū Palace.
After Lord Fù was confirmed dead,
they sent out funeral notices to the feudal lords.
Lord Fù initially made his eldest son Zhāng crown prince,
but later obtained Wú Wá,
loved her,
and did not leave (her chamber) for several years.
She bore a son Hé,
so he deposed Crown Prince Zhāng and established him.
(Hé,
is King Huìwén.)
When his love waned;
he pitied the former crown prince,
wanted to make both kings,
hesitated and could not decide,
hence the turmoil arose.
4 In Qín, Lóu Huǎn was dismissed as chancellor,
and Wèi Rǎn replaced him.
1 Qín defeated the Wèi army at Xiè.
1 Hán’s Gōngsūn Xǐ and a man from Wèi attacked Qín.
(The Wèi history writes ‘a man’,
because the general was insignificant.)
(General,
pronounced jí liàng fān.)
(Bái,
a surname.)
During the Spring and Autumn period,
Qín had Bái Yǐbǐng.)
(Ráng,
pronounced rén yáng fān.)
(Change,
pronounced gōng héng fān.)
(Xiàng,
pronounced xī liàng fān.)
They beheaded 240,000,
captured Gōngsūn Xǐ,
and captured five cities.
The King of Qín appointed Bái Qǐ as Guówèi.
(During the Warring States period,
there were Guówèi,
and Jùnwèi.
Yìng Shào said: ‘Wèi’ means pacifying those below from above,
all military officials used this title.)
(Defeat,
pronounced bǔ mài fān.)
2 The King of Qín sent a letter to the King of Chǔ:
“Chǔ betrays Qín,
Qín will lead the feudal lords to attack Chǔ,
I hope Your Majesty will prepare your troops.”
(Prepare,
means manage,
organize.)
(Send,
pronounced yú jì fān.)
(Betray,
pronounced pú mèi fān.)
The King of Chǔ was worried,
so he again made peace and kinship with Qín.
(Peace and kinship means forming peace to become close.)
(Again,
pronounced fú yòu fān,
also pronounced as usual.)
1 King Xiāng of Chǔ welcomed a bride from Qín.
Your servant Guāng says: How extreme is Qín’s lack of virtue,
killing the father and coercing the son;
(meaning King Huái of Chǔ was detained in Qín and died in distress,
the King of Qín again sent a letter to King Xiāng,
coercing him with military might.)
Dù Yù said: Compete,
means strong.
Some say: Compete,
means contend,
meaning unable to contend with Qín.)
King Xiāng of Chǔ’s father died in Qín,
that is a country of enmity,
yet he endured shame and married into it.
If the ruler of Chǔ truly possessed the Way,
and his ministers truly had capable men,
even if Qín were strong,
how could it oppress them!
How excellent is Xún Qīng’s discussion:
“As for the Way,
if used well, a hundred lǐ of land can stand independently;
if used poorly, even Chǔ’s six thousand lǐ becomes a servant to enemies.”
Therefore, if a ruler does not strive to attain the Way but broadly possesses power,
that is why he is endangered.
1 In Qín, Wèi Rǎn pleaded illness and was dismissed,
and the visiting minister Zhú Shòu was made chancellor.
(Zhú,
a surname.
Zuǒzhuàn records that Zhèng had a senior official Zhú Zhīwǔ.)
1 Qín attacked Hán,
and captured Wǎn.
(Wǎn,
formerly the state of Shēnbó.
Bǎn Zhì states: Wǎn County belonged to Nányáng Commandery;
in Táng it was Nányáng County of Dèng Prefecture.)
(Wǎn,
pronounced yú yuán fān.)
In Qín, Zhú Shòu was dismissed.
Wèi Rǎn again became chancellor,
enfeoffed at Ráng and Táo,
called Ráng Hóu.
Also enfeoffed Prince Shì at Wǎn,
and Prince Kuī at Dèng.
1 Wèi ceded four hundred lǐ of Hé dōng territory,
(Hé dōng territory,
probably refers to lands near the river in Ānyì, Dàyáng, Púbǎn, and Xiè County.)
(Bǎn,
pronounced fǎn.)
(Xiè,
pronounced xià mǎi fān.)
and Wǔsuì territory,
(which Qín gave to Hán in the eighteenth year.)
(Give,
read as ‘yǔ’.)
2 In Wèi, Máng Mǎo began to be valued through deceit.
1. The Qin State's Dàliángzào Bái Qǐ and Guest Minister Cuò attacked the State of Wei,
reaching Zhǐ,
and captured sixty-one cities, both large and small.
Dàliángzào,
refers to the excellent among the Dàshàngzào.
Dàshàngzào,
is the sixteenth rank of nobility in Qin.
Zhǐ,
pronounced zhǐ.
Zhǐ County,
according to Bān Zhì, belonged to the Hénèi Commandery;
during the Táng dynasty, it was Jìyuán County of Mèng Prefecture.
1. In winter,
the tenth month,
the King of Qin proclaimed himself the Western Emperor,
and sent an envoy to establish the King of Qí as the Eastern Emperor,
intending to make a pact with him to jointly attack the State of Zhào.
Sū Dài came from the State of Yān,
and the King of Qí said:
"Qín has sent Wèi Rǎn to confer the title of Emperor upon me,
what do you think of this?"
He replied:
"I hope Your Majesty will accept it but not use the title.
If Qín uses the title,
and the world is at peace with it,
then Your Majesty may use it,
and it will not be too late.
'Not too late',
means it is still timely.
If the world detests it,
Your Majesty should then not use the title,
thereby winning over the world,
this is a great advantage.
Moreover, which is more beneficial, attacking Zhào or attacking the tyrannical Sòng?
The tyrannical Sòng,
see the twenty-ninth year below.
Dispatch troops to attack the tyrannical Sòng,
and if Sòng is taken, then Chǔ, Zhào, Liáng, and Wèi will all be fearful.
In this way, we honor Qín in name but cause the world to hate it,
which is what is called 'using humility to achieve honor'."
The ancients had a saying:
"Those who humble themselves will be honored by others."
After proclaiming himself Emperor for two days, he returned the title.
He returned the title of Emperor and did not use it.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān,
also pronounced as the original character.
Lǚ Lǐ went from Qí to Qín.
The Surname Compendium says: Tàiyuè was a minister trusted by Yǔ,
thus he was enfeoffed as Marquis Lǚ,
and later this became a surname.
The ancient character for the spine bone, lǚ, was originally written as
"Lǚ".
He resumed calling himself King.
2. Qín attacked Zhào,
capturing Dùyáng.
Xú Guǎng said:
"Dù",
in one version is written as
"Gěng".
According to Bān Zhì,
Gěngyáng was within the boundaries of Yúcì County in Tàiyuán Commandery,
while Dùyáng County belonged to Fúfēng,
with a note stating: The Dù River flows south into the Wèi River.
The Shī says
"from Tǔ".
Shī Gǔ's annotation states: The Bó version of the Shī: Bái Tǔ, Jū, Qī.
The Qí version of the Shī writes
"from Dù",
saying that Gōng Liú came from Dí and settled in the lands of Dù, Jū, and Qī.
It also says: In Fúfēng, Xúnyì County has the Bīn Township,
which was the capital of Gōng Liú.
If this is accurate,
then Dùyáng is near Xúnyì,
bordering the territories of Shàngjùn and Běidì.
The territory of Zhào extended west to Fūshī in Shàngjùn,
so perhaps at that time it also included Dùyáng!
Jū,
pronounced qī yú fān.
Xún,
pronounced xū lún fān.
Bīn,
pronounced bǐ pín fān.
3. Qín attacked Zhào,
capturing Xīnyuán and Qūyáng.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: According to the chronological tables and Kuòdìzhì,
the old city of Qūyáng was forty lǐ west of Jìyuán County in Huái Prefecture,
and Xīnyuán was near Qūyáng,
but the exact location is not clear.
I note that according to Bān Zhì,
Mount Wángwū is in Yuán County of Hédōng,
where the Yǎn River originates,
flowing east to become the Jì River.
The Shuǐjīng states: The Jì River originates from Mount Wángwū in Yuán County, Hédōng, as the Yǎn River.
The annotation says: The Jì River has a second source emerging from flat land northwest of Wēn.
The river has two sources,
the eastern source emerges northeast of Yuánchéng,
where Duke Wén of Jìn won over Yuán with trust,
that is this city.
It is commonly called Jìyuánchéng because it is where the second source of the Jì River emerges.
Therefore, it is also called Jìyuán City.
Thus, Jìyuán is not far from Yuán.
It seems that Xīnyuán is Yuán County in Hédōng;
because the county seat was relocated,
its new settlement was called Xīnyuán.
Yuán,
pronounced yú yuán fān.
Jì,
pronounced zǐ lǐ fān.
Yǎn,
pronounced yǐ zhuǎn fān.
Xiáng,
pronounced hù jiāng fān.
Chóng,
pronounced zhí lóng fān.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān.
1. Qín's Sīmǎ Cuò attacked the Hénèi region of the State of Wei.
The Hàn dynasty's Hénèi Commandery was the territory of Wei's Hénèi,
which Qín later incorporated into the Hédōng Commandery.
Mèngzǐ records King Huì of Liáng saying:
"If there is famine in Hénèi, I move its people to Hédōng,
and move grain from Hédōng to Hénèi."
It seems that in the State of Wei,
Hédōng and Hénèi were two separate commanderies.
Cuò,
pronounced qī gè fān,
also qiān gù fān.
Qín expelled its people and returned them to Wei.
2. Qín defeated the Hán army at Xiàshān.
3 In Sòng, a sparrow gave birth to a zhān bird in the corner of the city wall.
"Zhān bird,"
Liú Xiàng's Shuō Yuàn writes it as
"zhān."
Zìlín says: It is a type of sparrowhawk.
Lù Jī says: The zhān resembles a sparrowhawk,
greenish-yellow in color,
with a swallow-like chin and hooked beak,
it flaps its wings facing the wind,
then uses the wind to fly swiftly,
striking doves, pigeons, swallows, and sparrows to eat them.
Zōu,
pronounced zǐhóu fān,
means corner.
Gōu,
pronounced gǔhóu fān.
Shǐ,
refers to the Grand Historian's office,
those in charge of divination.
"Auspicious.
An inauspicious person finds his inauspiciousness auspicious.
He will surely dominate the world."
King Kāng of Sòng was pleased,
raised troops and destroyed Téng,
attacked Xuē,
Bān Zhì: Gōngqiū County in Pèi Commandery,
was the ancient state of Téng.
Shuǐjīng Zhù: Téng City is west of Fán County.
Táng Zhì,
Téng County belongs to Xúzhōu.
Xuē is the fiefdom of Lord Mèngcháng.
Fán,
pronounced pí,
also pronounced as the character's usual reading.
He captured five cities,
defeated Chǔ in the south,
taking three hundred lǐ of land,
defeated the Wèi army in the west,
and became an enemy state to Qí and Wèi,
thus growing even more confident in his hegemony.
Desiring his hegemony to be achieved quickly,
he thus shot at heaven and whipped the earth,
cut down the altars of soil and grain and burned them to destruction.
The Records say: Gònggōngshì had a son named Gōulóng,
who could level water and earth,
thus he was worshipped as the god of soil.
Lièshānshì's son was named Zhù,
he was the god of grain,
worshipped from the Xià dynasty and earlier;
Zhōu's Qì was also the god of grain,
worshipped from the Shāng dynasty onward.
From the Hàn dynasty onward,
Xià Yǔ was paired as the official god of soil,
Hòujì was paired as the official god of grain.
Zhōulǐ Zhù: Shèjì,
are the gods of soil and grain.
Gòng,
read as gōng.
Xià,
pronounced hù yǎ fān.
He held all-night drinking parties in his chambers,
when the people inside the chambers shouted "Long live!",
then those in the hall responded,
those below the hall responded again,
those outside the gate responded again,
extending throughout the state,
and none dared not shout "Long live!"
The people of the world called him
"the Jié of Sòng."
Meaning his tyranny and violence were like Jié.
The people scattered,
the city could not be defended.
The King of Sòng fled to Wèi,
and died in Wēn.
Wēn,
was the fief of Sū Fènshēng, Minister of Justice of Zhōu.
Bān Zhì,
Wēn County belongs to Hénèi Commandery.
Sòng was thus destroyed.
Mǐn,
read as mǐn.
1 The King of Qín met with the King of Chǔ in Wǎn,
and met with the King of Zhào in Zhōngyáng.
Bān Zhì,
Zhōngyáng County belongs to Xīhé Commandery.
Shuǐjīng Zhù: Wénshuǐ passes east of the old city of Zīshì County in Tàiyuán,
forming Wén Lake;
Wén Lake water then passes east of the old city of Zhōngyáng County.
2 Qín's Méng Wǔ attacked Qí,
capturing nine cities.
Fēngsú Tōng: The Lord of Dōngméng took Méng Mountain as his clan name.
3 King Mǐn of Qí, having destroyed Sòng, became arrogant,
then invaded Chǔ in the south,
invaded the Three Jìn in the west,
wanting to annex the two Zhōu,
and become the Son of Heaven.
Hú Xuǎn remonstrated with righteous criticism,
and was executed at Tán Qú.
Hú,
is a surname.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
Jìn had Hú Tū, Hú Máo, and Hú Yǎn, father and sons.
Zuǒzhuàn: Duke Jiǎn of Qí drank with women at Tán Terrace.
Tán Qú,
likely refers to the road leading to Tán Terrace.
Ěryǎ: A road reaching four directions is called a qú.
Xuǎn,
pronounced kuàng wǎn fān,
also kuàng yuǎn fān.
Zhuó,
pronounced cè lüè fān,
means to behead.
He was killed at Dōng Lǘ.
Zuǒzhuàn: When Jìn besieged Qí,
Zhōu Chuò attacked the gate at Dōng Lǘ.
Dù Yù's commentary says: The eastern gate of Qí.
King Zhāo of Yān day and night comforted and cared for his people,
making them increasingly wealthy and prosperous,
then discussed with Yuè Yì about attacking Qí.
Yuè Yì said:
"Qí,
is the remnant of a hegemonic state,
with vast territory and numerous people,
it is not easy to attack alone.
If Your Majesty truly wishes to attack it,
it would be best to form an alliance with Zhào as well as Chǔ and Wèi."
Thereupon he sent Yuè Yì to ally with Zhào,
separately sent envoys to connect with Chǔ and Wèi,
and also ordered Zhào to entice Qín with the benefits of attacking Qí.
The feudal lords resented the arrogance and tyranny of the King of Qí,
and all vied to join in the plan with Yān to attack Qí.
1. The King of Yān mobilized all his troops,
appointing Yuè Yì as the Supreme General.
The Supreme General
is akin to the Marshal of the Spring and Autumn period.
Shuài,
pronounced as suǒ lèi fān.
Wèi,
is an official title from Qín.
Sī Lí,
is his name.
Some say: Sī,
is a surname;
Lí,
is a given name.
Sī,
is a tribe of the southwestern barbarians of Shǔ,
and thus became a surname.
Shuài,
is read as shuài.
Yuè Yì led the combined armies of Qín, Wèi, Hán, and Zhào to attack Qí.
King Mǐn of Qí gathered all the forces within his state to resist them,
and they fought west of the Jì River,
where the Qí army suffered a major defeat.
Yuè Yì sent back the armies of Qín and Hán,
divided the Wèi army to seize the territory of Sòng,
and deployed the Zhào army to capture Héjiān.
Qín and Hán were far separated from Qí,
so he first sent their armies back.
The territory of Sòng was close to Wèi,
so he ordered them to seize it.
Héjiān was close to Zhào,
so he devised a strategy for Zhào to take it.
This arrangement,
was beyond what others could achieve.
The territory of Sòng,
was land Qí had taken after destroying Sòng.
He pursued the defeated enemy deep into their territory.
Jù Xīn said:
"Qí is large and Yān is small.
Relying on the assistance of the feudal lords to defeat their army,
it would be appropriate to seize their border cities in a timely manner to benefit ourselves.
This is a long-term advantage.
Now, passing by without attacking,
using deep penetration as a pretext,
does no harm to Qí,
brings no benefit to Yān, and instead creates deep enmity.
You will surely regret it later."
Yuè Yì said:
"The King of Qí boasts of his achievements and flaunts his abilities,
his plans do not reach his subordinates,
he dismisses the worthy and virtuous,
trusts flatterers and sycophants,
his governance is cruel and oppressive,
and the common people resent him.
Now that his army is completely defeated,
if we take advantage of this situation,
his people will surely rebel,
and internal turmoil will erupt.
Then Qí can be taken.
If we do not seize this opportunity,
and wait for him to regret his past wrongs,
reform his ways, care for his subordinates, and pacify his people,
then it will be difficult to plan against him."
So he advanced his army deep into Qí.
The people of Qí indeed fell into great chaos and lost their bearings.
Nán lǜ,
means difficult to plan against.
Shī dù,
means losing their normal composure.
Yuè Yì entered Línzī,
took treasures and sacrificial vessels,
and transported them to Yān.
The King of Yān personally went to the banks of the Jì River to reward the army,
distributing rewards and feasting the soldiers;
he enfeoffed Yuè Yì as the Lord of Chāngguó.
According to Bān Zhì,
Chāngguó County belonged to Qí Commandery.
Enfeoffing Yì as Lord of Chāngguó,
was because he was able to make the state of Yān flourish.
The King of Qí fled and went to Wèi,
where the ruler of Wèi vacated his palace to house him,
addressed him as sovereign, and provided all necessities.
The King of Qí was disrespectful,
so the people of Wèi encroached upon him.
The King of Qí left and fled to Zōu and Lǔ,
with an arrogant demeanor;
Zōu and Lǔ would not admit him,
so he went to Jǔ.
Jǔ,
was the state of the Viscount of Jǔ in the Spring and Autumn period,
which Qí had destroyed.
According to Bān Zhì,
Jǔ County belonged to Chéngyáng Kingdom,
which was the capital of the kingdom.
Sòng Bái said: King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed Zīyú of the Yíng surname, a descendant of Shǎohào, at Jǔ,
initially establishing the capital at Jìjīn City,
located forty lǐ southeast of present-day Gāomì County.
During the Spring and Autumn period, it moved to Jǔ.
In the second year of Duke Yǐn,
the people of Jǔ entered Xiàng.
The commentary states: present-day Chéngyáng Jǔ County.
Jǔ, from its initial enfeoffment, had twenty-three rulers,
and was destroyed by King Jiǎn of Chǔ.
In Hàn times, it was Jǔ County,
the capital of the King of Chéngyáng.
Jǔ,
pronounced jū yù fān.
He then became the chancellor of Qí.
Nào Chǐ wanted to divide the territory of Qí with Yān,
so he seized King Mǐn and enumerated his crimes.
Shǔ his crimes.
Yán Shìgǔ said: Shǔ,
pronounced suǒ jù fān;
Sòng Qí said: suǒ zhǔ fān.
"Between Qiānshèng and Bóchāng,
an area of several hundred lǐ square,
blood rained down, staining clothes.
Hàn established Qiānshèng Commandery,
and Bóchāng County belonged to it.
Later Hàn changed Qiānshèng Commandery to Lè'ān Kingdom.
The Treatise of the Thirteen Provinces states: Chāng River,
its flow is gentle,
hence the name Bóchāng.
According to Táng records,
both Qiānshèng and Bóchāng counties belonged to Qīngzhōu.
Shèng,
pronounced shéng zhèng fān.
Yù,
pronounced wáng yù fān.
Falling from above is called yù.
He said:
"I know of it."
"Between Yíng and Bó,
the earth split open down to the springs.
According to Bān Zhì,
Yíng and Bó counties belonged to Tàishān Commandery.
He said:
"I know of it."
"There was a person who wept before the palace gate,
but when sought, he could not be found.
When he left, his voice was heard.
Did Your Majesty know of this?"
He said:
"I know of it."
Nào Chǐ said:
"The blood rain staining clothes,
was Heaven's warning;
the earth splitting to the springs,
was Earth's warning;
the person weeping before the gate,
was a warning from man.
Heaven, Earth, and man all gave warnings,
yet Your Majesty did not know to take heed.
Jiè,
is the same as jiè;
jiè,
means to warn and admonish.
Máo Huàng said: Words of warning and admonition are called jiè.
This means Heaven, Earth, and man all warned and admonished you.
Then he killed the king at Gǔlǐ.
Gǔlǐ,
is a place name within Jǔ,
near the ancestral temple of Qí.
Xúnzǐ commented on this, saying: The state,
is the most advantageous position in the world.
If one holds it with the Way,
then there is great security,
great glory,
and it is a source of accumulated excellence.
If one does not hold it with the Way,
then there is great danger,
great burden,
and having it is worse than not having it;
and at its extreme,
even wishing to be a commoner,
one cannot attain it.
King Mǐn of Qí and King Xiàn of Sòng are examples of this.
Therefore, he who governs a state: if he establishes righteousness, he becomes a true king;
if he establishes trust, he becomes a hegemon;
if he establishes cunning and deceit, he perishes.
To lead a state by invoking ritual and righteousness, and to do nothing to harm them.
To commit a single act of injustice,
to kill a single innocent person,
and thereby gain the world—
a benevolent person would not do such a thing.
Firmly upholding the mind and the state,
and doing so as steadfastly as this.
Firmly,
like the appearance of a falling stone;
meaning that in upholding the mind and upholding the state,
one is as firm as a rock.
Firm,
pronounced as lì gè fān.
Then one promotes righteous men.
The reason for establishing laws and punishments in the state,
is to promote righteous laws.
What the ruler most earnestly desires,
Máo Huǎng said: Earnestly,
means "like,"
means "this."
Then one promotes righteous intentions.
If it is like this,
then those below will look up to those above with righteousness,
and the foundation is settled.
Foundation
settled and the state is settled,
the state settled and the world is settled.
Therefore it is said: To use the state to advance righteousness,
in one day it becomes clear,
as with Tāng and Wǔ.
Foundation,
means base,
means root.
To establish a base for earth is called foundation;
to establish a root for wood is also called foundation.
Clear,
means bright.
Even if virtue has not yet been fully attained,
even if righteousness has not yet been fully realized,
yet the principles of the world are roughly in harmony,
Yáng Jìng said: Roughly means having rhythm.
Promise,
is the sound of a person's response.
Trust,
is when people have no doubts and hearts are sincere.
When government orders have been issued,
even if gains and losses are observed,
they do not deceive their people;
when agreements have been settled,
even if gains and losses are observed,
they do not deceive their allies;
Allies,
means companions.
That is, the allied states mentioned below.
Then the army is strong and the city walls are solid,

when the state's foundation is clearly unified,
Yáng Jìng said: This
"foundation"
should be read as
"foundation."
Now it is said that this
"foundation"
character follows the above annotation,
so-called words of the people of Qí,
its meaning is also understandable.
Clear,
means evident.
Even if in a remote and backward state,
its power moves the world,
as with the Five Hegemons.
This is what is called establishing trust and becoming a hegemon.
To lead a state by invoking profit and gain,
not striving to expand its righteousness,
nor aligning its trustworthiness,
seeking only profit;
internally, they do not hesitate to deceive their people to seek small gains,
externally, they do not hesitate to deceive their allies to seek great gains.
Internally, they do not rectify what they possess,
yet constantly desire what others have.
If it is like this,
then ministers and commoners will all treat their superiors with deceitful hearts.
The superiors deceive their subordinates,
the subordinates deceive their superiors,
then the upper and lower are divided.
If it is like this,
then enemy states will look down on them,
and allied states will suspect them,
schemes and plots are practiced daily and the state cannot avoid danger and decline,
reaching the extreme and perishing,
as with Qí Mǐn and Xuē Gōng.
Therefore, using the strength of Qí,
not to cultivate ritual and righteousness,
not to base it on government and education,
not to unify the world,
but constantly engaging in alliances and external expeditions.
Therefore, though strong,
in the south it could defeat Chǔ,
in the west it could subdue Qín,
in the north it could defeat Yān,
in the center it could conquer Sòng.
According to the Records of the Grand Historian,
in the tenth year of King Mǐn of Qí,
he attacked Yān,

in the twenty-third year,
together with Qín, he defeated Chǔ at Chóngqiū,

together with Hán and Wèi, he attacked Qín,

Defeat,
pronounced as bǔ mài fān.
Subdue,

Yān,
pronounced as yīn jiān fān.
And when they attacked,
it was like shaking dry leaves,

Examine,
means to investigate,
also means to evaluate.
Only because they did not follow ritual and righteousness but followed schemes and plots.
These three,
are what enlightened rulers carefully choose,

Clear,
means to understand clearly.
Those who do not choose well are controlled by others.
2 Yuè Yì heard that in Zhù
town there was a worthy man named Wáng Zhú.
He ordered his army not to enter within thirty *lǐ* of Zhù town.
He sent someone to invite Zhú,
but Zhú declined and did not go.
A man of Yān said:
"If you do not come,
we will slaughter Zhù town!"
Zhú said:
"A loyal minister does not serve two lords;
a chaste woman does not take a second husband.
The state is destroyed and the lord is gone;
I cannot preserve them,
and now you wish to coerce me with weapons.
I would rather die
than live without righteousness!"
He then hung his neck from a tree branch,
and with a forceful leap, broke his neck and died.
*Jīng*
means to strangle,
to hang.
*Jǐng*,
pronounced *jū yǐng fān*,
means the stem of the head.
*Zì fèn*
means to leap up and throw oneself down.
*Dòu*,
pronounced *dà tòu fān*,
means neck.
All the cities of Qí fled in panic upon hearing the news.
Yuè Yì disciplined the Yān army,
forbade plundering,
sought out the reclusive scholars of Qí,
honored them, and treated them with courtesy.
He lightened taxes and levies,
abolished harsh laws,
restored the former governance,
and the people of Qí rejoiced.
He then sent the left army to cross Jiāodōng and Dōnglái;
Jiāodōng
was made a kingdom in the Hàn dynasty.
According to the *Shuǐ Jīng*: The Jiāo River originates from Jiāo Mountain in Qiánzōu County of Lángyá,
flows north past Jiāodōng and Xiàmì,
and further north past Dānglì County in Dōnglái before entering the sea.
East of the Jiāo River was the Kingdom of Jiāodōng,
west of the Jiāo River was the Kingdom of Jiāoxī.
Dōnglái
was the state of the Lái clan in the Spring and Autumn period,
and the Hàn dynasty established Dōnglái Commandery.
*Yé*,
pronounced *yē*.
They captured Lángyá;
Lángyá
was established as a commandery in the Qín dynasty,
its territory extending east to the sea,
and south reaching the Huái River.
They stationed troops at Ā and Juàn to connect with the Wèi army;
the annotation for Héjì is already seen in the first volume, the fifteenth year of King Ān,
but it only covers the section where the Jì River enters the Hé and overflows to form the Xíng.
Now, according to the *Shuǐ Jīng*: The Jì River flows east from the Xíng Marsh to the west of Chéngshì County in Jìyīn,
where it divides into two channels: the southern channel is the Hé River,
flowing southeast to Hùlù County in Shānyáng,
where it merges with the Sì River.
The northern channel flows northeast into the Jùyě Marsh,
passes northeast through the western border of Shòuliáng County in Dōng Commandery,
goes north past Xūchāng and Gǔchéng to the Sìdú Jīn estuary in Línyì County,
where it merges with the Hé River.
This likely refers to the Qí territory lying between the Hé and Jì Rivers.
Refer to the previous annotation on Jìxī for clarity.
*Jì*,
pronounced *zǐ lǐ fān*.
Ā,
refers to Dōng'ē;
Juàn,
refers to Juànchéng.
*Juàn*,
pronounced *juàn*.
*Chéng*,
pronounced *shéng zhèng fān*.
*Hé*,
pronounced *kē*.
The central army occupied Línzī and secured the Qí capital.
They offered sacrifices to Duke Huán and Guǎn Zhòng in the suburbs,
erected markers at the gates of worthy men,
and built a tomb for Wáng Zhú.
Wáng Zhú's tomb is likely in Zhù.
*Fēng* means to enfeoff as a lord.
Jì
was the capital of Yān.
According to Bān's *Treatise*,
Jì County belonged to Guǎngyáng Kingdom.
In the Táng dynasty, it was the seat of Yōuzhōu;

According to the *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù*: In the northwest corner of Jì City, there is Jì Hill,
hence the name.
*Yān*,
pronounced *yīn jiān fān*.
*Jì*,
pronounced *jì*.

all made into commanderies and counties.
3 The King of Qín, the King of Wèi, and the King of Hán met in the capital.

2 During the rebellion of Nào Chǐ in Qí,
King Mǐn's son, Fǎ Zhāng, changed his name and became a servant in the household of Tàishǐ Jiǎo in Jǔ.

*Qiè*
means privately,

*Yì*,
pronounced *yú jì fān*.
*Sì*,
pronounced *xiáng lì fān*.
Wángsūn Gǔ followed King Mǐn,

means the gate of a village.

Later people discussing Yuè Yì

3 King of Zhào obtained the He's Jade Disc of Chǔ.
A man of Chǔ named Biàn Hé obtained a raw jade stone,
and presented it to King Lì of Chǔ.
The king had a jade artisan examine it,
who said:
"It is stone."
The king considered Hé deceitful,

When King Wǔ ascended the throne,
Hé presented it again.
The jade artisan again said:
"It is stone."
The king again considered it deceitful and had his right foot amputated.
When King Wén ascended the throne,
Hé then embraced the raw stone and wept at the foot of Jīng Shān.
The king heard of this,
had a jade artisan work the raw stone,
and obtained a treasure.
Therefore, it was named
"The Jade Disc of Hé."
Ěryǎ states: When the body (flesh) is twice the size of the hole, it is called a bì (disc).
Its outer circle symbolizes Heaven,
its inner square symbolizes Earth.
(Qín) requested to exchange it for fifteen cities.

wishing to give it,

Lìn,
read as lì rèn fān.
"If Qín requests the disc with cities and Your Majesty does not consent,

it is better to consent and place the burden on Qín.
(This means) making Qín bear the fault.
If Qín's cities are not handed over,

Liàng,
pronounced liàng.

Zhòng,

means to match.
Ǒu,

"Use these to balance each other."

means three,
to arrange in threes,
to interpose.

was one who won the people,

was one who governed,

Therefore, those who cultivate ritual become kings,

1 Qín attacked Zhào,
capturing two cities.
1 Qín attacked Zhào,

Shuài,
read as shuài, meaning to lead.
Shào,
read as shào, meaning young.
Gǒng,
read as gǒng.
Nǎn,
read as nǎn.
Gaining its populace would not suffice to strengthen one's army.
Nevertheless,
those who attack it bear the name of regicide.

if one were to make a marsh deer wear a tiger's skin,

Splitting Chǔ's territory

1 Qín's Bái Qǐ defeated the Zhào army,

West of Qiān county in Fúfēng is the great Lǒng mountain,

Cuò,
read as cuò,
also read as cù.
Qiān,
read as qiān.
Huán,
read as huán.
He captured it.

Qián,
read as qín.

was Cáo Wèi's Xīnchéng,
the land of Táng's Fánglíng commandery.
1 Qín's Bái Qǐ attacked Chǔ,

2 The King of Qín sent an envoy to inform the King of Zhào,

The King of Zhào wished not to go.
Lián Pō and Lìn Xiàngrú planned and said:
(The surname genealogy: The surname Lián descends from Dàlián, great-grandson of Zhuānxù.
Pō,
read as pō.)
"If the King does not go,

Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān,
also pronounced as the character itself.
Fǒu,
pronounced fāng jiǔ fān.
Yùn,
pronounced yú fěn fān.
Chéng,
pronounced shí zhēng fān.
Xù,
pronounced xū jù fān.
Xiàngrú said:
"Within five steps,

Jǐng,
pronounced jū yǐng fān.
Jiàn,

The lord drove the chariot into the market,
where Hóu Shēng got down to see his friend Zhū Hài.
The surname genealogy states: The Zhū clan originally came from Gāoyáng,
and Zhōu enfeoffed their descendants in Zhū;
later, when it was destroyed by Chǔ,
the descendants removed the radical 邑 and adopted the surname Zhū.
Thus, he stood for a long time,
conversing with his friend,
pì nì,
meaning not looking directly.
Pì,
pronounced pǐ yì fān.
Nì,
pronounced yán jì fān.
The lord's expression grew even more amiable;
then Hóu Shēng bid farewell to his friend and boarded the chariot,
arriving at the lord's residence.
The lord led Hóu Shēng to sit in the seat of honor,
introduced him to all the guests,
and the guests were all astonished.
Suǒyǐn states: Zàn,
means to announce.
Refers to announcing Hóu Shēng to all the guests.
Biàn,
is the same as biàn (everywhere).
The wife of Lord Píngyuán of Zhào,
was the elder sister of Lord Wújì.
Lord Píngyuán's envoys, with their caps and canopies, came one after another to Wèi,
reproaching the lord, saying:
"The reason I attached myself through marriage
was because of your high righteousness,
and your ability to urgently aid those in distress.
Now Hándān may surrender to Qín at any moment, yet Wèi's rescue has not arrived.
Even if you, my lord, disregard and abandon me,
do you not pity your own elder sister?"
The lord was troubled by this,
repeatedly requesting King Wèi to order Jìn Bǐ to rescue Zhào,
and his retainers and debaters used myriad arguments to persuade him,
but the king ultimately refused to listen.
The lord then gathered his retainers,
prepared over a hundred chariots and riders,
intending to rush into battle and die in Zhào;
passing by Yímén,
he saw Hóu Shēng.
Hóu Shēng said:
"My lord, go forth with effort,
but this old minister cannot accompany you!"
The lord departed,
traveled several lǐ,
felt unsettled,
because Hóu Shēng neither accompanied him
nor devised a plan for him.
Hóu Shēng laughed and said:
"I knew you would return, my lord!
Now, with no other plan, you wish to rush against the Qín army—
wú tā duān,
meaning having no other ingenious strategy to initiate action.
What merit could there be in that?"
The lord bowed twice and asked for a plan.
Hóu Yíng dismissed others and said:
"I have heard that Jìn Bǐ's military tally is in the king's bedchamber,
and Rú Jī is the most favored,
capable of stealing it.
I have heard that you, my lord, avenged her father's death for Rú Jī,
and she is willing to die for you without hesitation.
If you, my lord, truly make the request,
you will obtain the tiger tally.
The tiger,
a fierce and mighty beast,
was thus used for the military tally.
The Hàn Dynasty had bronze tiger tallies.
Rescuing Zhào in the north,
repelling Qín in the west,
this would be an achievement worthy of the Five Hegemons."
The lord followed his advice,
and indeed obtained the military tally.
As the lord was about to depart,
Hóu Shēng said:
"A general in the field
may not always accept the sovereign's orders.
The words of Sūn Wǔzǐ.
Jiàng,
pronounced jí liàng fān.
Lìng,
pronounced lì dìng fān.
If you request again,
the situation will become perilous.
My friend Zhū Hài,
that man is a man of great strength,
you can take him with you.
If Jìn Bǐ complies,
excellent;
if not,
have him strike Jìn Bǐ down!"
Thereupon, the lord requested Zhū Hài to accompany him.
Arriving at Yè,
Jìn Bǐ matched the tallies,
grew suspicious,
raised his hand, looked at the lord, and said:
"I command a hundred thousand troops stationed at the border,
yet now you come alone in a single chariot to replace me.
How can this be?"
Zhū Hài concealed a forty-catty iron hammer in his sleeve,
struck and killed Jìn Bǐ with it.
The lord then took command of the troops and issued an order to the army:
"If both father and son are in the army,
the father may return!
If both brothers are in the army,
the elder brother may return!
If one is an only son without brothers,
return to support your family!"
He thus selected eighty thousand elite soldiers,
led them, and advanced.
Wáng Hé had long besieged Hándān without capturing it,
and when the other states came to rescue,
he suffered several defeats in battle.
Lord Wǔ'ān heard of this and said:
"The king did not heed my advice,
and now what is the situation?"
Bái Qǐ believed Hándān was not easily taken,
and Wáng Hé's army indeed met with setbacks,
hence his remark.
Angered,
the king forced Lord Wǔ'ān to take command.
Lord Wǔ'ān claimed to be gravely ill,
refusing to rise.
1 In the tenth month,
the Marquis Wǔ'ān was stripped of his rank and made a common soldier,
and was exiled to Yīnmì.
Rú Chún said: According to the law: If one is guilty and loses his official rank,
he is called a common soldier.
Master Yán Gǔ said: This means his noble rank was taken away,
and he was ordered to become a common soldier;
it means making him join the ranks of the soldiers.
According to Bān Zhì,
Yīnmì County belonged to Āndìng Commandery,
the ancient state of Mì,
which is what the Odes refers to
as "the people of Mì were not respectful"
Kuòdìzhì: The old city of Yīnmì,
was west of Chúngǔ County in Jīng Prefecture,
the ancient state of the Mìxū clan.
More troops were dispatched to encamp beside Fénchéng.
Fénchéng,
was the city of Línfén County in Hédōng during the Hàn,
still far from Hándān.
The Qín probably stationed troops here,
to provide support for Wáng Yǐ.
Kuòdìzhì: The old city of Línfén,
was thirty-five lǐ northeast of Zhèngpíng County in Jiàng Prefecture.
Before he could depart,
the allied states attacked Wáng Yǐ,
and Yǐ was repeatedly forced back,
with messengers arriving daily,
so the King sent someone to escort the Marquis Wǔ'ān,
not allowing him to remain within Xiányáng.
The Marquis Wǔ'ān left Xiányáng through the western gate for ten lǐ,
reaching Dùyóu.
Shuǐjīngzhù: The old channel of the Wèi River passed south of Ānlíng,
and beside the channel was the Dùyóu Pavilion,
and it also passed north of Wèichéng.
Qín's Xiányáng,
was the Hàn's Wèichéng.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: The present-day Xiányáng County city,
was originally the Dùyóu of Qín times,
located thirty-five lǐ northwest of Yōng Prefecture.
Yóu,
is pronounced yóu.
Yōng,
is pronounced yòng.
"When Bái Qǐ was exiled,
his mind was still resentful and he had more to say."
The King then sent an envoy to bestow upon him a sword,
and the Marquis Wǔ'ān then committed suicide.
The people of Qín pitied him,
and villages and towns all made sacrifices to him.
The Lord Wújì of Wèi inflicted a great defeat on the Qín army below Hándān,
and Wáng Yǐ lifted the siege of Hándān and fled.
Zhèng Ānpíng, being hard-pressed by Zhào,
led twenty thousand men and surrendered to Zhào,
and because of this, the Marquis Yìng incurred guilt.
Zhèng Ānpíng hid Fàn Jū to meet Wáng Jī,
and through this, Jū entered Qín and became chancellor,
so Jū guaranteed and appointed Ānpíng and employed him.
Now that Ānpíng surrendered to Zhào,
Jū therefore incurred guilt because of this.
Qín law: Guaranteeing and appointing someone who proves unworthy incurs the same crime.
Yìng,
is pronounced yīng.
Since Lord Wújì had preserved Zhào,
he did not dare return to Wèi,
but stayed in Zhào with his retainers,
sending a general to lead his army back to Wèi.
The King of Zhào consulted with Lord Píngyuán,
and decided to enfeoff the Lord with five cities.
The King of Zhào swept the path and personally went to welcome him,
performing the rites of a host,
guiding the Lord to the western steps.
The Lord walked sideways, declining and yielding,
and ascended by the eastern steps.
The Lǐjì Qūlǐ records: The host goes to the eastern steps,
the guest goes to the western steps.
If the guest is of lower status,
then he goes to the host's steps.
Shàng,
is pronounced shǎng.
Zuì,
is the ancient character for 'crime'.
Qín Shǐhuáng because
the character "zuì"
resembled
the character "huáng"
changed it to
"zuì".
Having no merit towards Zhào.
The King of Zhào drank with the Lord until dusk,
but could not bring himself to offer the five cities,
because the Lord was modest and yielding.
The King of Zhào gave Hào to the Lord as his bath and grooming estate.
Master Yán Gǔ said: Whenever one speaks of a bath and grooming estate,
it means using its taxes to supply the necessities for bathing and grooming.
Hào,
is pronounced hū gè.
Dù Yòu said: The Lord Xìnlíng's estate was in present-day Nínglíng County of Sòng Prefecture.
Lord Xuē was living in hiding at the home of a beverage seller,
and the Lord wished to meet him;
the two men refused to see him,
so the Lord then went incognito on foot to associate with them.
Lord Píngyuán heard of this and criticized it.
The Lord said:
"I heard of Lord Píngyuán's worthiness,
so I turned my back on Wèi to save Zhào.
Now, those whom Lord Píngyuán associates with
are merely for show of grandeur,
he does not seek true men of worth.
That I, Wújì, associate with these two men,
I still fear they may not want me,
and Lord Píngyuán actually considers it shameful!"
He prepared his baggage intending to leave.
'Prepared his baggage' means,
preparing his traveling gear.
Then he stopped.
Lord Píngyuán wished to enfeoff Lǔ Lián,
because he had refuted Xīnyuán Yǎn's words about making Qín emperor.
He ultimately refused to accept.
He also offered a thousand pieces of gold as a longevity gift for Lǔ Lián,
Lǔ Lián laughed and said:
"What is valued in a true man of worth of the world,
is to resolve troubles, dispel difficulties, and untangle confusion for others without taking anything.
If there is taking,
that is the business of merchants!"
Then
he declined Lord Píngyuán and left,
never to be seen again for the rest of his life.
2 The crown prince of Qín's consort was called Lady Huáyáng,
probably because she received a bath and grooming estate at Huáyáng,
and thus took it as her title.
Huá,
is pronounced huà.
Xià Jī gave birth to a son, Yìrén.
Yìrén was a hostage in Zhào;
Qín repeatedly attacked Zhào,
and the people of Zhào did not treat him with courtesy.
Yìrén, as a grandson by a concubine held hostage among the feudal lords,
his carriages and supplies were not ample.
Zhāng Yàn said: A young son is called a 'nie' son.
Hé Xiū said: A 'nie' son,
is a base son,
a son not born of the principal wife is called 'nie'.
Master Yán Gǔ said: 'Nie',
means a son by a concubine.
Tángyùn says: It is like a tree having side shoots.
Yìrén was a son by a concubine to the crown prince of Qín,
and a grandson by a concubine to the King of Qín.
Niè,
is pronounced yú liè.
Suǒyǐn says: 'Jìn' here,
means goods,
it is appropriate to follow Xiǎo Yán and read it as 'jìn',
ancient characters often borrowed and used it.
Jìn,
is pronounced cái rèn.
A great merchant from Yángdí, Lǚ Bùwéi, happened to be in Hándān.
He saw him,
and said:
"This rare commodity can be hoarded!"
He then went to see Yìrén,
and persuaded him, saying:
"I can make your family great!"
Yìrén laughed and said:
"You should first make your own family great!"
Lǚ Bùwéi said:
"You do not understand.
My family's greatness awaits the greatness of your family."
Yìrén understood what he meant,
and invited him to sit,
speaking deeply with him.
Lǚ Bùwéi said:
"The King of Qín is old.
The Crown Prince favors Lady Huáyáng,
but she has no son.
You have over twenty brothers.
Zǐxī holds the
state of Qín's inheritance,
and Shì Cāng assists him.
Genealogy: The surname Shì,
descendants of Jìn's Shì Wěi.
You are not particularly favored,
having long been a hostage among the feudal lords.
Once the Crown Prince ascends the throne,
you will not be able to contend for the succession."
Yìrén said:
"What then is to be done?"
Lǚ Bùwéi said:
"The one who can establish the rightful heir
is solely Lady Huáyáng.
Although I am poor,
I ask to use a thousand pieces of gold to travel west on your behalf,
to establish you as the heir."
Yìrén said:
"If your plan succeeds,
I ask to share the state of Qín with you."
Lǚ Bùwéi then gave five hundred pieces of gold to Yìrén,
ordering him to befriend guests.
He further used five hundred pieces of gold to buy rare objects and curiosities,
and taking them himself, he went west.
He met the elder sister of Lady Huáyáng,
and presented the rare objects to the Lady,
taking the opportunity to praise the worthiness of Yìrén,
saying his guests were from all under heaven,
and that he constantly wept day and night, longing for the Crown Prince and the Lady,
saying:
"Yìrén regards the Lady as his heaven!"
The Lady was greatly pleased.
Lǚ Bùwéi then had her elder sister persuade the Lady, saying:
"Those who serve others with their beauty,
when their beauty fades, their favor wanes.
Now, you are favored but have no son.
If you do not, while in the prime of your splendor, early on attach yourself to one among the princes who is worthy and filial,
and raise him as the rightful heir,
then when your beauty fades and favor wanes,
even if you wish to utter a single word,
will it still be possible?
Now, Yìrén is worthy,
and he himself knows that as a middle son
he cannot become the rightful heir.
If you, Lady, truly seize this moment to elevate him,
then this son Yìrén, who has no state, will gain a state,
and you, Lady, who have no son, will gain a son.
Then you will enjoy favor in Qín for the rest of your life."
The Lady considered this right,
and seizing an opportunity, spoke to the Crown Prince, saying:
"Yìrén is exceptionally worthy."
Máo Huǎng said: Jué (絕),
means extraordinary, surpassing.
It signifies a vast distance.
She then wept and said:
"I, your concubine, am unfortunate to have no son.
I wish to take Yìrén and establish him as my son,
so that I may entrust myself to him!"
The Crown Prince agreed,
and with the Lady, carved a jade tally,
pledging to make him the heir.
He then sent generous gifts to Yìrén,
and requested Lǚ Bùwéi to be his tutor.
Yìrén's reputation flourished among the feudal lords.
Lǚ Bùwéi took a Hándān singing girl of exceptional beauty to live with him.
The character "qǔ" (娶)
"to marry"
should, according to the Records of the Grand Historian, be written as
"qǔ" (取) "to take".
Hándān,
pronunciation: Hán Dān.
Yìng Shào said: Shēn (娠),
means the stirring and conception of pregnancy.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: Yì Jiāng was just shēn (pregnant).
Mèng Kāng said: Shēn (娠),
pronunciation: shēn,
In the Book of Hàn,
"shēn" (娠)
is often written as
"shēn" (身) "body",
these are ancient and modern forms of the character.
Master Yán (Yán Shígǔ) said: Mèng's explanation is correct.
The Book of Hàn all uses shēn (娠) for the character meaning pregnancy.
Yì Jiāng was just zhèn (震) "stirred",
here zhèn is the zhèn (震) meaning "to stir/agitate",
not written as shēn (娠).
He saw her and requested her.
Lǚ Bùwéi pretended to be angry,
but later presented her,
she was pregnant and after a full year gave birth to a son, Zhèng.
Yìrén then made her his wife.
During the siege of Hándān,
the people of Zhào wanted to kill him.
Yìrén and Lǚ Bùwéi distributed six hundred catties of gold to the guards,
escaped, and fled to the Qín army,
thus managing to return.
Yìrén, wearing Chǔ clothing, went to see Lady Huáyáng.
Chǔ clothing means
clothing in the style of Chǔ people.
Some say: Chǔchǔ (楚楚),
means splendid attire.
"I am a man of Chǔ,
I should treat you as my son."
She therefore changed his name to Chǔ.
1. A Qín general, Jiū, attacked Hán.
Jiū,
Shǐjì Zhèngyì: pronunciation Jì Qiú.
Kāng (a commentator) said: pronunciation Jū Yóu.
He beheaded forty thousand.
He attacked Zhào,
captured over twenty counties,
and beheaded or captured ninety thousand.
King Nǎn was afraid,
turned against Qín,
and formed a vertical alliance with the feudal lords,
leading the elite troops of all under heaven out of Yīquè to attack Qín,
ordering that no one be allowed to reach Yángchéng.
The King of Qín sent General Jiū to attack Western Zhōu. King Nǎn entered Qín,
kowtowed and accepted blame,
offering all his thirty-six towns,
with a population of thirty thousand.
Qín accepted his offering,
and sent King Nǎn back to Zhōu.
That year,
King Nǎn passed away.
Huángfǔ Mì said: Zhōu had thirty-seven kings in total,
lasting eight hundred and sixty-seven years.
